113918.q: Why is castor oil not poisonous, even though it is pressed from poisonous seeds?
a: The poison stays in the pressed residue
The oil is mixed with sugar
113918.e: Ricin does not dissolve in oil. It stays behind in the press cake, so the oil itself is not poisonous.
113918.m: When the seeds are pressed, the poison ricin stays in the residue and not in the oil.

113919.q: What was castor oil often used for as a home remedy in the past?
113919.e: Castor oil strongly stimulates the bowels. In the past it was often taken for constipation.
113919.m: Castor oil is a strong laxative.

113920.q: How can you easily recognise the castor oil plant in a garden?
a: By its large, hand-shaped, often red leaves
113920.e: The castor oil plant has large leaves lobed like a hand, often reddish in colour. That is why it is planted as an ornamental plant.
113920.m: The castor oil plant has large, hand-shaped leaves.

113921.q: How does ricin act in the body's cells?
a: It stops the production of proteins
113921.e: Ricin paralyses the ribosomes, which make proteins. Without new proteins, the cells die.
113921.m: Ricin stops cells from making proteins.

113922.q: Why is chewing castor oil seeds more dangerous than swallowing whole seeds?
a: Only the broken seed coat releases the poison
Chewed seeds get bigger in the mouth
Whole seeds contain no poison at all
113922.e: The hard seed coat partly holds back the poison. If the seed is chewed, the ricin gets into the body much more easily.
113922.m: Chewed castor oil seeds are especially dangerous.

113923.q: Where are you most likely to find the castor oil plant in Switzerland?
a: As an ornamental plant in gardens and parks
Growing wild in the high mountains
113923.e: The castor oil plant comes from warmer regions. In Switzerland it is planted as an ornamental plant because of its large, often reddish leaves.
113923.m: In Swiss gardens the castor oil plant grows as an ornamental plant.

113924.q: Which region does the oleander originally come from?
113924.e: The oleander grows wild in the Mediterranean region, often on riverbanks. In Switzerland it is usually kept in pots on balconies and terraces.
113924.m: The oleander comes from the Mediterranean.

113925.q: Which organ does oleander poison mainly affect?
113925.e: Oleander contains so-called cardiac glycosides. They disrupt the heartbeat.

113926.q: A small child has eaten oleander leaves. What should you do straight away?
a: Wait and see if anything happens
113926.e: Oleander is very poisonous. In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps around the clock on 145; in an emergency you call 144.
113926.m: In cases of poisoning, the number 145 helps.

113927.q: Which parts of the oleander are poisonous?
113927.e: The leaves, flowers, stems, seeds and sap are poisonous. Even the smoke when it is burnt can be harmful.
113927.m: All parts of the oleander are poisonous.

113928.q: Why does an oleander in Switzerland usually need protecting in winter?
a: It needs lots of fertiliser in winter
It only flowers in the dark
113928.e: The oleander comes from mild regions. In hard frost it freezes, so it is brought indoors to a bright, cool place.
113928.m: Oleander must be protected from hard frost.

113929.q: What is true of the oleander's leaves?
a: It sheds all its leaves in autumn
It has no leaves at all
113929.e: The oleander keeps its narrow, leathery leaves all year. This helps it survive well in the dry Mediterranean climate.
113929.m: The oleander is an evergreen shrub.

113930.q: What do oleander leaves look like?
113930.e: The oleander has narrow, long, leathery leaves. This means it loses little water in the dry Mediterranean climate.
113930.m: The oleander has narrow, leathery leaves.

113931.q: What should you do with the branches after pruning an oleander?
a: Not burn them and not feed them to animals
113931.e: Smoke and dried leaves are poisonous too. So cuttings belong neither on a fire nor with pets.
113931.m: You do not burn oleander branches or give them to animals.

113932.q: How do the flowers of the angel's trumpet hang on the plant?
a: Flat plates lie on the ground
113932.e: The large trumpet-shaped flowers hang downwards. On the related thorn apple, by contrast, they point upwards.
113932.m: Angel's trumpets have large, hanging trumpet-shaped flowers.

113933.q: Which continent do angel's trumpets come from?
113933.e: Angel's trumpets come from South America. In Switzerland they are popular potted plants.
113933.m: The angel's trumpet comes from South America.

113934.q: Which plant family does the angel's trumpet belong to?
113934.e: The angel's trumpet belongs to the nightshade family, like deadly nightshade and the potato. It contains poisons similar to those of deadly nightshade.
113934.m: The angel's trumpet is a member of the nightshade family.

113935.q: Which parts of the angel's trumpet are poisonous?
113935.e: All parts of the angel's trumpet contain poisons such as scopolamine and atropine. These substances confuse the senses and strain the heart.
113935.m: The whole angel's trumpet is poisonous.

113936.q: Why is it dangerous to use angel's trumpets as a drug?
a: The amount of poison is almost impossible to judge
The plant has no effect at all
It is only harmful to animals
113936.e: The amount of poison varies greatly from plant to plant. It causes confusion, hallucinations and a racing heart, which can be fatal.
113936.m: Using angel's trumpets as a drug is life-threatening.

113937.q: When do angel's trumpet flowers smell strongest?
a: In the evening and at night
113937.e: The flowers give off a strong scent mainly in the evening. In their homeland this attracts pollinators that are active at night.
113937.m: Angel's trumpets smell especially strong in the evening.

113938.q: What is true of angel's trumpet species in the wild?
a: They are considered extinct in the wild
They are very common in the Alps
They only live in the sea
113938.e: All species are considered extinct in the wild. They only survive because people plant them.
113938.m: Today angel's trumpets are found almost only in gardens.

113939.q: What growth form does the angel's trumpet have?
113939.e: Angel's trumpets grow as woody shrubs or small trees. In pots they often grow more than two metres tall.
113939.m: The angel's trumpet grows as a shrub or small tree.

113940.q: Roughly when does ragwort (St James's wort) start to flower?
a: Around St James's Day at the end of July
113940.e: Its German name refers to St James's Day on 25 July. Around this time the yellow flowers are in full bloom.
113940.m: Ragwort flowers around St James's Day in July.

113941.q: What colour are the flowers of ragwort?
113941.e: The plant has many small yellow flower heads. It belongs to the daisy family.

113942.q: For which animals is ragwort especially dangerous?
a: For horses and cattle in pastures
113942.e: Ragwort contains poisonous substances called pyrrolizidine alkaloids. If horses or cattle eat it again and again, their liver is damaged.
113942.m: Ragwort is poisonous to grazing animals.

113943.q: Which organ do the poisons in ragwort mainly damage?
113943.e: The poisons gradually destroy the liver. Because the damage builds up, even small amounts are harmful over a long time.

113944.q: Why is ragwort in hay especially dangerous for horses and cattle?
a: In hay the warning bitter taste is missing
In hay the plant becomes sweeter and bigger
In hay the plant grows spines
In hay the poison multiplies greatly
113944.e: Animals often avoid fresh plants because of their bitter taste. When dried they notice this less, but the poison remains.
113944.m: Animals eat the poisonous plant in hay because it tastes less bitter there.

113945.q: The black and yellow striped caterpillar of the cinnabar moth eats poisonous ragwort. What happens as a result?
a: It becomes poisonous to birds itself
113945.e: The caterpillars store the plant's poison in their bodies. Their warning colours show birds that they are not good to eat.
113945.m: The cinnabar moth caterpillar eats ragwort and becomes poisonous itself.

113946.q: Why is the plant called “groundsel” in German, meaning “old man's herb”?
a: The white seed hairs look like an old man's hair
Only old people are allowed to pick it
It lives for very many years
It grows outside old people's homes
113946.e: After flowering, the seeds carry tufts of white hair. They look like the white hair of an old man.
113946.m: The white seed hairs gave the plant its German name.

113947.q: How are the seeds of ragwort spread?
113947.e: The seeds have fine little hairy parachutes like dandelions. With these they fly far on the wind, for example along roadsides.
113947.m: The wind spreads the seeds of ragwort.

113948.q: Which of these vegetables is wild garlic most closely related to?
113948.e: Wild garlic belongs to the onion genus, like chives, onions and garlic. That is why it has a similar taste.
113948.m: Wild garlic is a relative of chives and onions.

113949.q: What kind of substances give wild garlic its typical smell?
113949.e: When the leaves are crushed, substances containing sulphur are produced. They are responsible for the sharp, spicy smell.
113949.m: The smell of wild garlic comes from sulphur compounds.

113950.q: Why is the smell test unreliable when picking wild garlic?
a: The garlic smell sticks to your hands
Wild garlic has no smell at all
The smell can only be noticed at night
113950.e: After a few leaves, your fingers themselves smell of garlic. Then you can no longer smell the difference with a wrong leaf.
113950.m: When picking wild garlic, check each leaf separately, because your hands smell of garlic.

113951.q: What does wild garlic grow from again every spring?
a: From a bulb in the ground
From the branches of a shrub
113951.e: Wild garlic has a slender bulb in the ground. It stores nutrients there for the next spring.
113951.m: Wild garlic grows every year from a bulb in the ground.

113952.q: How do the leaves of wild garlic grow?
a: Each leaf has its own stalk coming out of the ground
Two leaves wrap around each other at the base
Many leaves sit without stalks in a rosette
The leaves grow on a tall stem
113952.e: With wild garlic, each leaf comes out of the ground separately on its own stalk. This helps to tell it apart from lily of the valley and autumn crocus.
113952.m: Each wild garlic leaf grows separately on its own stalk.

113953.q: What happens to wild garlic leaves a few months after they appear?
113953.e: Two to three months after they appear, the leaves turn yellow as the ground warms up. In summer there is hardly anything of the wild garlic to be seen above ground.
113953.m: In summer the wild garlic leaves disappear again.

113954.q: Where does wild garlic prefer to grow?
113954.e: Wild garlic likes shady, damp deciduous woods and floodplains. There it often forms large carpets.
113954.m: Wild garlic grows in damp deciduous woods.

113955.q: What do wild garlic flowers look like?
a: White little stars in a cluster
113955.e: Many small white star-shaped flowers sit together at the top of a stem. They flower in spring in the woods.
113955.m: Wild garlic has white star-shaped flowers in a cluster.

113956.q: What is the safest rule when picking wild plants such as wild garlic?
a: Only pick what you know for certain
Only take leaves at the edge of the wood
113956.e: Many poisonous plants look like edible plants. If you are unsure, leave the plant where it is.
113956.m: Only eat plants that you recognise with complete certainty.

113957.q: Who answers the calls at Tox Info Suisse?
113957.e: At Tox Info Suisse, doctors and other medical specialists give advice. The advice is free.
113957.m: At Tox Info Suisse, medical specialists give advice.

113958.q: Which short number do you dial in Switzerland in a case of poisoning to reach Tox Info Suisse?
113958.e: In Switzerland you can reach Tox Info Suisse around the clock on 145. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade. If someone is unconscious, you dial 144 straight away.
113958.m: In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on 145.

113959.q: Who can contact Tox Info Suisse?
a: Members of the public and specialists
113959.e: Tox Info Suisse advises members of the public as well as doctors, hospitals and companies. Anyone can get in touch about poisoning.
113959.m: Anyone can contact Tox Info Suisse about poisoning.

113960.q: When can you reach Tox Info Suisse?
113960.e: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night, including public holidays, on 145. The centre has existed since 1966.
113960.m: Tox Info Suisse helps around the clock.

113961.q: About how many enquiries did Tox Info Suisse receive in 2025?
113961.e: At the beginning there were around 2,000 enquiries a year. In 2025 there were 44,736 consultations, which is more than 40,000.
113961.m: Tox Info Suisse answers more than 40,000 enquiries every year.

113962.q: Which group accounts for about 40 per cent of enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
113962.e: Small children put lots of things in their mouths. That is why around 40 per cent of enquiries concern children under five.
113962.m: Many cases of poisoning involve small children.

113963.q: What should you NOT do after someone has swallowed a poisonous plant?
113963.e: Making someone vomit can cause extra harm. It is better to call 145 straight away and follow the instructions.
113963.m: In a case of poisoning, do not make anyone vomit; call 145 instead.

113964.q: Why should you keep a piece of the plant after plant poisoning?
a: So that specialists can identify it
So that you can plant it later
So that it can act as an antidote
So that it does not wilt
113964.e: If it is known which plant was eaten, the danger can be judged better. That is why you show a piece or a photo of it.
113964.m: A piece of the plant helps to judge the poisoning correctly.

113965.q: What does Tox Info Suisse help with?
113965.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice around the clock on 145 when someone has swallowed or touched something poisonous.
113965.m: Tox Info Suisse helps with poisoning, phone 145.

113966.q: What is the long extension of a nerve cell that passes on signals called?
113966.e: The axon carries the electrical signal away from the cell body to the next cell. It can be very long.
113966.m: The axon carries signals away from the nerve cell.

113967.q: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
a: They receive signals from other cells
They store fat for the winter
113967.e: Dendrites are like antennae. They pick up signals from other nerve cells and pass them to the cell body.
113967.m: Dendrites are the antennae of the nerve cell.

113968.q: Roughly how many nerve cells does the human brain have?
113968.e: Researchers have estimated the number of nerve cells in the brain at about 86 billion. That is about ten times more than the number of people living on Earth.
113968.m: Our brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.

113969.q: What is the myelin sheath around many axons for?
a: It speeds up the passing on of signals
113969.e: The myelin sheath insulates the axon like the covering of a cable. This makes the signals jump along faster.
113969.m: Myelin insulates nerve fibres and makes signals travel faster.

113971.q: How do nerve cells pass on information?
113971.e: Nerve cells produce tiny electrical signals that travel through the body very quickly. That is how the message “hot” gets from your hand to your brain, for example.
113971.m: Nerve cells pass on information as electrical signals.

113972.q: What are the cells in the brain called that support and supply the nerve cells?
113972.e: Glial cells hold the nerve cells in place, supply them and in some cases form the myelin sheaths. Without them, the brain could not work.
113972.m: Glial cells are the helper cells of the nerve cells.

113973.q: What is the cord of nerve fibres in the back called that connects the brain and the body?
113973.e: The spinal cord runs protected inside the spine. It carries signals back and forth between the brain and the rest of the body.
113973.m: The spinal cord connects the brain and the body.

113974.q: Roughly how long can the longest nerve cells in humans be?
113974.e: Some nerve cells reach from the spinal cord to the toes. Their axon can therefore be about a metre long.
113974.m: The longest nerve cells reach from the back to the toes.

a: The point of contact between two nerve cells
A blood vessel in the brain
113975.e: At the synapse, a signal is passed from one nerve cell to the next or to a muscle cell. The word means “connection”.
113975.m: Synapses are the connection points between nerve cells.

113976.q: What are the messenger substances called that pass on signals at a synapse?
113976.e: Neurotransmitters are released by one cell and attach to the next cell. This passes the signal on.
113976.m: Neurotransmitters carry signals across the synapse.

113977.q: What is the tiny gap between two cells at a synapse called?
113977.e: There is a very narrow gap between the cells. The messenger substances have to cross it to pass the signal on.
113977.m: At the synapse, the messenger substances cross the synaptic cleft.

113978.q: Where are the messenger substances stored at the end of an axon?
113978.e: The messenger substances are kept in tiny bubbles called vesicles. When a signal arrives, the bubbles release their contents into the gap.
113978.m: Messenger substances are stored in small bubbles.

113979.q: What happens when a nerve releases a messenger substance at a skeletal muscle?
113979.e: At the junction between nerve and muscle, the messenger substance acetylcholine is released. This makes the muscle contract.
113979.m: A messenger substance makes the muscle contract.

113980.q: Which messenger substance is closely linked with the brain's reward system?
113980.e: Dopamine is released when something goes better than expected. It plays an important role in learning and motivation.
113980.m: Dopamine is part of the brain's reward system.

113981.q: What do inhibitory messenger substances do in the brain?
a: They slow down the activity of nerve cells
113981.e: Inhibitory messenger substances such as GABA slow nerve cells down. Excitatory messenger substances such as glutamate, on the other hand, stimulate them.
113981.m: Inhibitory messenger substances slow down nerve cells.

113982.q: What does the Greek word that “synapse” comes from mean?
113982.e: The British researcher Charles Sherrington introduced the term in 1897. It describes the point where two nerve cells connect.

113983.q: Roughly how many synapses are there in the human brain?
113983.e: Each nerve cell often has thousands of points of contact. In total, the number of synapses is estimated at about 100 trillion.
113983.m: There are about 100 trillion synapses in the brain.

113984.q: What is the bridge of nerves called that connects the two halves of the cerebrum?
113984.e: The corpus callosum consists of many millions of nerve fibres. The two halves of the brain exchange information through it.
113984.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

113985.q: Why is the surface of the cerebrum so heavily folded?
a: So that more cortex fits into the skull
So that the brain is lighter
So that less blood flows into it
So that the brain stays cooler
113985.e: The folds make the area of the cerebral cortex much larger. Even so, it still fits into the limited space of the skull.
113985.m: The folds increase the surface of the cerebral cortex.

113986.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are visual impressions mainly processed?
113986.e: The visual cortex is in the occipital lobe, right at the back of the head. The signals from the eyes go there.
113986.m: We see with the back part of the cerebrum.

113987.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum mainly processes the skin's sense of touch?
113987.e: The centre for body sensations is in the parietal lobe. Signals of touch, pressure and temperature from the skin arrive there.
113987.m: The sense of touch is processed in the parietal lobe.

113988.q: Which half of the cerebrum controls the movements of the right side of the body?
113988.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain controls the right side of the body and the other way round.
113988.m: The left half of the brain controls the right side of the body.

113989.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are important areas for planning and making decisions?
113989.e: The frontal lobe is right behind the forehead. It is important for planning, making decisions and controlling your own behaviour.
113989.m: The frontal lobe helps us plan and make decisions.

113990.q: In which part of the brain do thinking, learning and remembering mainly happen?
113990.e: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. Its cortex processes sensory impressions, and this is where we think, learn and remember.
113990.m: We think and learn in the cerebrum.

113991.q: What is the folded outer layer of the cerebrum with very many nerve cells called?
113991.e: The cerebral cortex is only a few millimetres thick but contains billions of nerve cells. Because of its colour, it is also called grey matter.
113991.m: The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the cerebrum.

113992.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum is the hearing centre?
113992.e: The auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe, at the side of the head, roughly level with the ears. Sounds and speech are processed there.
113992.m: The hearing centre is in the temporal lobe.

113993.q: What is the main job of the cerebellum?
113993.e: The cerebellum makes sure that movements are smooth and precise. It also helps you keep your balance.
113993.m: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

113994.q: Which part of the brain contains more than half of all nerve cells?
113994.e: The cerebellum is small, but tightly packed. It contains most of all the nerve cells in the brain.
113994.m: The small cerebellum contains most of the nerve cells.

113995.q: Why do drunk people often walk unsteadily and sway?
113995.e: Alcohol affects the cerebellum. Then balance and coordination are disturbed.
113995.m: Alcohol disrupts the cerebellum and with it your balance.

113996.q: In which kind of learning is the cerebellum especially involved?
a: Practising movements such as riding a bike
113996.e: The cerebellum helps to fine-tune movements through practice. This is how riding a bike, for example, becomes automatic over time.
113996.m: The cerebellum helps you practise movements.

113997.q: What does the Latin name “cerebellum” mean?
113997.e: Cerebrum means brain, and cerebellum is the form meaning “small”. So the cerebellum is literally the “little brain”.

113998.q: Which sign is typical when the cerebellum is damaged?
a: Loss of the sense of smell
113998.e: When the cerebellum is damaged, movements look wobbly and imprecise. Experts call this ataxia.
113998.m: Damage to the cerebellum makes movements unsteady.

113999.q: Where in the head is the cerebellum?
a: At the back, under the cerebrum
At the front, behind the forehead
At the top, under the crown
At the side, behind the ears
113999.e: The cerebellum is at the back of the head, below the cerebrum. It is connected to the brainstem.
113999.m: The cerebellum is at the back of the head, under the cerebrum.

114000.q: Which vital function does the brainstem control?
114000.e: The brainstem contains centres that control breathing and circulation. They work completely without conscious thought.
114000.m: The brainstem controls breathing and heartbeat.

114001.q: Which parts belong to the brainstem?
a: Frontal lobe, corpus callosum and cerebellum
114001.e: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata. The medulla oblongata leads into the spinal cord.
114001.m: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata form the brainstem.

114002.q: What is the brainstem connected to at its lower end?
114002.e: The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord. All the pathways between the brain and the body run through it.
114002.m: The brainstem connects the brain and the spinal cord.

114003.q: Which protective reflexes are controlled in the brainstem?
114003.e: Swallowing, coughing, sneezing and gagging are controlled by the brainstem. They protect the airways.
114003.m: The brainstem controls coughing and swallowing.

114004.q: Why is the brainstem considered the oldest part of the brain?
a: Very early vertebrates already had similar structures
It only forms in old age
114004.e: Fish, amphibians and reptiles also have a similar brainstem. It developed very early in the evolution of vertebrates.
114004.m: In evolutionary terms, the brainstem is the oldest part of the brain.

114005.q: Why is a serious injury to the brainstem so dangerous?
a: Vital functions such as breathing can fail
Afterwards you just cannot sing any more
It is not dangerous at all
114005.e: The brainstem controls breathing, heartbeat and circulation. If it fails, the body can no longer survive on its own.
114005.m: The brainstem is vital for life.

114006.q: What is a doctor checking when she shines a light into the eye and looks at the pupil?
a: Whether a reflex through the brainstem is working
Whether the corpus callosum is thick enough
114006.e: In light, the pupil gets smaller as a reflex. This pupil reflex runs through the brainstem.
114006.m: The pupil reflex shows whether the brainstem is working.

114007.q: Where in the head is the brainstem?
a: At the bottom of the brain, directly above the spinal cord
Right at the front behind the forehead
At the top under the skullcap
114007.e: The brainstem forms the lower part of the brain. It runs down into the neck, where it leads into the spinal cord.
114007.m: The brainstem is at the bottom of the brain.

a: The brain is made of plastic
The brain stays the same all your life
You can shape the brain like clay
114008.e: Neuroplasticity means that connections in the brain change through learning and experience. In this way, the brain is constantly adapting.
114008.m: Our brain changes when we learn.

114009.q: According to a well-known study, which part of the brain was larger in London taxi drivers?
114009.e: London taxi drivers learn thousands of streets by heart. In them, part of the hippocampus, which is important for spatial memory, was larger.
114009.m: Lots of practice at finding your way changes the hippocampus.

114010.q: What happens to the connection between two nerve cells that are often active at the same time?
114010.e: If two nerve cells are often active together, their connection gets stronger. That is why practice helps learning.
114010.m: Nerve cells that fire together wire together.

114011.q: What happens to rarely used connections in the brain?
a: They get weaker or are removed
They move into the spinal cord
114011.e: The brain removes connections that are hardly used. Connections that are used often, on the other hand, are strengthened.
114011.m: What we do not practise fades away in the brain.

114012.q: Why can people partly relearn lost abilities after a stroke?
a: Other brain areas take over tasks
114012.e: Thanks to neuroplasticity, healthy areas can take over the tasks of damaged areas. This takes a lot of training, for example in therapy.
114012.m: After a stroke, other brain areas can take over tasks.

114013.q: What did a study show in which adults practised juggling for three months?
a: Certain brain areas increased in volume
114013.e: After the training, certain areas of the cerebral cortex that see and process movement were larger. This shows that adults can change their brains too.
114013.m: Adults also change their brains when they practise something new.

114014.q: Which brain area is often also used by blind people when reading Braille?
114014.e: In blind people, the visual cortex is not needed for seeing. It can then help with feeling Braille.
114014.m: The brain can use unused areas for new tasks.

114015.q: At what stage of life can the brain change?
114015.e: In childhood the brain is especially easy to shape. But adults and older people can still learn new things too.
114015.m: We can learn new things throughout our lives.

a: The electrical activity of the brain
The blood pressure in the arms
114016.e: The EEG measures small changes in voltage caused by the activity of many nerve cells. The curves are called brainwaves.

114017.q: Since when has it been possible to record a person's brainwaves?
114017.e: The German doctor Hans Berger first recorded human brainwaves in Jena in 1924.
114017.m: The EEG in humans has existed for about 100 years.

114018.q: Where are the electrodes placed for a normal EEG?
a: On the soles of the feet
114018.e: For a normal EEG, electrodes are stuck or placed on the scalp, often using a cap. The measurement does not hurt.
114018.m: In an EEG, the electrodes sit on the scalp.

114019.q: What does the EEG show when someone who is awake relaxes and closes their eyes?
114019.e: When you are awake and relaxed with your eyes closed, even alpha waves appear. If you open your eyes, they usually become weaker.
114019.m: Relaxing with closed eyes shows up in the EEG.

114020.q: What do brainwaves look like in the EEG during deep sleep?
a: There are none, the brain is off
114020.e: In deep sleep the waves become very slow and large. They are called delta waves.
114020.m: In deep sleep the EEG shows slow, large waves.

114021.q: For which illness is the EEG especially helpful in diagnosis?
114021.e: In epilepsy, typical patterns often appear in the brainwaves. The EEG is therefore an important tool for diagnosis.

114022.q: In which unit do you state how fast brainwaves oscillate?
114022.e: Hertz states how many oscillations take place per second. Alpha waves oscillate about 8 to 13 times per second.
114022.m: The frequency of brainwaves is measured in hertz.

114023.q: What is the EEG used for in a sleep laboratory?
a: To determine the stages of sleep
114023.e: Brainwaves change depending on the stage of sleep. From the EEG, experts can tell whether someone is in light sleep, deep sleep or dream sleep.
114023.m: In a sleep lab, the EEG shows the stages of sleep.

114024.q: What is the correct order in a reflex arc?
a: Receptor, nerve, spinal cord, nerve, muscle
114024.e: A receptor picks up the stimulus and a sensory nerve carries it to the spinal cord. From there, a motor nerve carries the command to the muscle.
114024.m: A reflex arc runs from the sensory receptor through the spinal cord to the muscle.

114025.q: Why do reflexes happen especially quickly?
a: They are often switched in the spinal cord
They use the blood as a pathway
114025.e: With many reflexes, the signal does not have to go to the cerebrum first. The spinal cord switches straight to the muscle, which saves time.
114025.m: Reflexes are fast because the spinal cord reacts directly.

114026.q: Which inborn reflex makes newborn babies grip a finger tightly in their hand?
114026.e: If you touch the palm of a newborn baby, it closes its fingers firmly. This grasp reflex disappears in the first months of life.
114026.m: Newborn babies have a strong grasp reflex.

114027.q: What happens when you touch a hot hob?
a: You pull your hand away before you feel the pain
You feel pain first and then think
114027.e: The withdrawal reflex is triggered in the spinal cord. The pain signal takes longer to reach the cerebrum, so you feel the pain a little later.
114027.m: With heat, a reflex pulls your hand away even before you feel pain.

114029.q: What are the nerve pathways called that carry signals from the spinal cord to the muscles?
114029.e: Sensory nerves carry stimuli to the spinal cord. Motor nerves carry commands to the muscles.
114029.m: Motor nerves carry commands to the muscles.

114031.q: What does research say about the idea that there are “left-brained” and “right-brained” people?
a: It is a myth without evidence
114031.e: Studies found no evidence that some people mainly use one half of the brain. Both halves work together in almost all tasks.
114031.m: Everyone uses both halves of the brain.

114032.q: Which hand do about 90 per cent of people prefer?
a: A different one depending on the season
114032.e: About nine out of ten people are right-handed. Preferring one hand is an example of the halves of the brain being specialised in different ways.

114033.q: In which half of the brain are the most important language centres in the vast majority of right-handers?
114033.e: In the vast majority of right-handers, the left half of the brain is more important for language. This is a real specialisation, but not a personality type.
114033.m: In most people, language is mainly processed on the left.

114034.q: What connects the two halves of the brain?
114034.e: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibres. Through it, the two halves of the brain exchange information.
114034.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

114035.q: Why was the corpus callosum between the halves of the brain cut in some people?
114035.e: In very severe epilepsy, cutting it could stop seizures from spreading to both halves. These patients are called split-brain patients.
114035.m: Split-brain operations were meant to ease severe epilepsy.

114036.q: What does lateralisation of the brain mean?
a: The halves of the brain specialise in some tasks
The brain lies at the side of the head
One half of the brain is always asleep
114036.e: Some tasks are processed more strongly in one half of the brain, for example language, usually on the left. Even so, both halves work closely together.
114036.m: Lateralisation means the halves of the brain have different focuses.

114037.q: Which statement about creativity and the halves of the brain is true?
a: Creative thinking uses both halves of the brain
Creativity is only in the right half
Creativity is only in the left half
Creativity is only in the cerebellum
114037.e: In creative thinking, networks in both halves of the brain work together. The idea of a purely “right-brain” creativity is greatly simplified.
114037.m: Creativity comes from both halves of the brain working together.

114038.q: Which half of the brain is more involved in recognising faces in most people?
114038.e: When recognising faces, the right half of the brain is more active in most people. Even so, both halves work together.
114038.m: We recognise faces mainly with the right half of the brain.

114039.q: Which animal's brain did the Blue Brain Project mainly want to recreate digitally?
114039.e: The goal was a detailed digital reconstruction of the mouse brain. Mice are often studied in brain research.
114039.m: The Blue Brain Project focused on the mouse brain.

114040.q: Who mainly funded the Blue Brain Project?
114040.e: The project was mainly funded with money from the Swiss Confederation. It was based at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne, the EPFL.
114040.m: The Swiss Confederation funded the Blue Brain Project.

114041.q: Which cells did the Blue Brain Project rebuild on the computer?
114041.e: The brain consists of billions of nerve cells. The project rebuilt them on the computer as accurately as possible to understand how the brain works.
114041.m: The Blue Brain Project simulated nerve cells.

114042.q: What was the goal of the Blue Brain Project?
a: To rebuild and simulate a brain digitally
To build a brain out of metal
114042.e: The project wanted to rebuild brain tissue on the computer, nerve cell by nerve cell, and simulate it.
114042.m: The Blue Brain Project wanted to recreate a brain on the computer.

114043.q: What did the Blue Brain Project need to simulate brain tissue?
114043.e: Simulating many nerve cells takes an incredible number of calculations. That is why the project ran on supercomputers.

114044.q: Why is it so difficult to simulate a whole human brain on a computer?
a: It has about 86 billion nerve cells
It has only ten nerve cells
It is made only of water
114044.e: Each nerve cell is connected to thousands of others. This huge number is beyond even today's supercomputers. That is why the Blue Brain Project first simulated small pieces of brain tissue.
114044.m: The human brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.

114045.q: At which university was the Blue Brain Project based?
114045.e: The project started in 2005 at the EPFL in Lausanne and ran until the end of 2024. Later it also worked in Geneva.
114045.m: The Blue Brain Project belonged to the EPFL in Lausanne.

114046.q: Which large EU brain research project started in 2013 with the EPFL taking part?
114046.e: The Human Brain Project was a flagship project of the EU and ran from 2013 to 2023. The EPFL coordinated it in the early years.
114046.m: The Human Brain Project was a large EU brain research project.

114047.q: Which sensory cells in the eye are responsible for seeing colour?
114047.e: The cones make colour vision possible in bright light. They are packed especially closely in the middle of the retina.
114047.m: We see colours with the cones.

114048.q: Why do we hardly see colours at dusk?
a: Then mainly the rods are working
114048.e: In low light, mainly the light-sensitive rods are working. They cannot tell colours apart, so everything looks grey.
114048.m: At dusk we see almost only shades of grey with the rods.

114049.q: How many types of cones does a person with normal vision have?
114049.e: There are cones for red, green and blue light. From their signals, the brain puts together all colours.
114049.m: We have three types of cones for colour vision.

114050.q: Why does every eye have a blind spot?
a: That is where the optic nerve leaves the eye
That is where the pupil is
That is where the lens is thickest
That is where the eyelid is attached
114050.e: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye, there are no sensory cells. The brain fills this gap so cleverly that we do not notice it.
114050.m: At the blind spot, the optic nerve leaves the eye.

114051.q: How does the image on the retina compare with reality?
114051.e: The lens projects the surroundings upside down onto the retina. Only the brain makes sure that we see the world the right way up.
114051.m: The brain turns the retina image the right way round for us.

114052.q: Which fifth basic taste is there besides sweet, sour, salty and bitter?
114052.e: Umami is Japanese and means something like “delicious”. It describes the savoury taste of, for example, stock or mature cheese.
114052.m: Umami is the savoury fifth basic taste.

114053.q: In which organ in the inner ear are sounds turned into nerve signals?
114053.e: The cochlea contains hair cells that are moved by sound. They turn the vibrations into nerve signals.
114053.m: The cochlea turns sound into nerve signals.

114054.q: What do optical illusions show about our perception?
a: The brain actively interprets sensory impressions
We see everything exactly as it is
114054.e: Optical illusions happen because the brain completes and interprets images based on experience. So perception is not simply a copy of the world.

114055.q: According to George Miller, roughly how many units can short-term memory hold at once?
a: About seven, plus or minus two
114055.e: In 1956 George Miller described the “magical number seven”. Newer research sometimes even assumes only about four units.
114055.m: Short-term memory holds only a few things at once.

114056.q: Roughly how long does information stay in short-term memory without repeating it?
a: About a thousandth of a second
114056.e: Without repetition, the contents of short-term memory are lost after about half a minute. If you repeat something, you hold on to it longer.
114056.m: Without repeating, we forget short-term memory contents after seconds.

114057.q: What is the easiest way to remember the phone number 0791234567?
a: Only the first and the last digit
114057.e: In groups, many digits take up fewer places in short-term memory. Experts call this chunking.
114057.m: If you group information, you can remember more.

114058.q: What does the brain do during sleep with what you learned during the day?
114058.e: During sleep, what you learned is replayed and transferred to long-term memory. That is why enough sleep is important for learning.
114058.m: Sleep helps you remember what you have learned.

114059.q: What is it called when someone can no longer remember new experiences after a brain injury?
114059.e: In memory loss, also called amnesia, new experiences no longer reach long-term memory. Short-term memory can still work.
114059.m: Without long-term memory, experiences stick only briefly.

114060.q: What is the memory called that holds information briefly while working on it, for example in mental arithmetic?
114060.e: Working memory holds intermediate results while you keep calculating. Baddeley and Hitch presented the model for it in 1974.
114060.m: Working memory helps us with mental arithmetic.

114061.q: Why do people often remember the last words well after a list is read aloud?
a: They are still in short-term memory
They are always the longest words
They are already in long-term memory
114061.e: The words heard last are still fresh in short-term memory. This is called the recency effect.
114061.m: You often remember the last words of a list well because they are still fresh.

114062.q: Which learning method helps most to keep things from short-term memory in the long term?
114062.e: If you go over material several times with breaks in between, you store it better in long-term memory. Cramming once is forgotten faster.
114062.m: Repeating with breaks helps memory most.

114063.q: What does the abbreviation REM in REM sleep stand for?
114063.e: REM stands for “Rapid Eye Movement”. In this sleep phase, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the closed eyelids.
114063.m: REM stands for the rapid eye movements during sleep.

114064.q: In which sleep phase do we dream particularly vividly and in pictures?
114064.e: People woken from REM sleep usually report vivid, story-like dreams. Dreams also occur in other phases, but they are usually fainter there.
114064.m: We have our most vivid dreams in REM sleep.

114065.q: What happens to most skeletal muscles during REM sleep?
114065.e: In REM sleep, the skeletal muscles are largely paralysed. This stops us actually carrying out the movements from our dreams.
114065.m: In REM sleep, the muscles are relaxed so that we do not act out our dreams.

114066.q: Why is REM sleep also called “paradoxical sleep”?
a: The brain is almost as active as when awake
You sleep with your eyes open
You do not breathe at all
114066.e: Although the body is deeply asleep, the brain in REM sleep shows a pattern of activity similar to being awake. This apparent contradiction gave the phase its name.
114066.m: In paradoxical sleep, the body is still but the brain is very active.

114067.q: Roughly what share of a night does REM sleep make up in adults?
114067.e: In healthy adults, REM sleep makes up around a fifth to a quarter of sleeping time. We spend most of the night in non-REM sleep.
114067.m: Adults spend about a fifth to a quarter of the night in REM sleep.

114068.q: Who spends a particularly large amount of sleeping time in REM sleep, about half?
114068.e: In newborn babies, active sleep, which corresponds to REM sleep, makes up about half of their sleep. This share decreases as they get older.
114068.m: Babies spend much more time in REM sleep than adults.

114069.q: When in the night do the REM phases last longest?
a: They are always the same length
114069.e: The first REM phase of the night is often only a few minutes long. The REM phases get longer from cycle to cycle, which is why we often remember dreams in the morning.
114069.m: The REM phases get longer and longer as the night goes on.

114070.q: Roughly how many REM phases do you have in a night?
114070.e: A sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes and usually ends with a REM phase. In one night, you go through 4 to 6 such cycles.
114070.m: There are several REM phases each night.

114071.q: How do heartbeat and breathing typically behave during REM sleep?
114071.e: In REM sleep, pulse and breathing vary more than in calm deep sleep. This fits with the high activity of the brain in this phase.
114071.m: In REM sleep, heartbeat and breathing become more irregular.

114072.q: How do brain waves change in deep sleep?
114072.e: If you measure brain activity in deep sleep, large, slow waves appear. The brain is then particularly calm.
114072.m: In deep sleep, the brain oscillates slowly.

114073.q: In which part of the night is deep sleep most common?
a: In the first half of the night
In the second half of the night
114073.e: The longest deep sleep phases occur in the first sleep cycles. Towards morning there is hardly any deep sleep, but more REM sleep.
114073.m: We get most of our deep sleep in the first half of the night.

114074.q: Which hormone is released in larger amounts mainly during deep sleep?
114074.e: The pituitary gland releases a lot of growth hormone, especially in the first deep sleep phases. It is important for growth and the repair of tissue.
114074.m: In deep sleep, the body releases a lot of growth hormone.

114075.q: How do you usually feel when you are woken from deep sleep?
114075.e: It is hard to wake up from deep sleep, and you need a few minutes to think clearly. This state is called sleep inertia.
114075.m: People woken from deep sleep are often groggy.

114076.q: How do pulse and blood pressure typically change in deep sleep?
114076.e: In deep sleep, the body is at its most relaxed. Heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing become slow and even.
114076.m: In deep sleep, the heart and circulation calm down.

114077.q: Which task for learning is particularly linked to deep sleep?
114077.e: In deep sleep, things learned during the day, such as vocabulary and facts, are consolidated in the memory. That is why sleep helps after learning.
114077.m: In deep sleep, the brain consolidates what it has learned.

114078.q: How does the share of deep sleep change with increasing age?
a: It disappears by the age of 10
114078.e: Children and teenagers have a lot of deep sleep. In older people there is much less of it, and sleep becomes lighter and is interrupted more often.
114078.m: With age, there is less deep sleep.

114079.q: Which sleep phase is considered the most restorative for the body?
114079.e: In deep sleep, the body is at its most relaxed. It recovers, repairs tissue and releases growth hormone.

114080.q: Roughly how long does a complete sleep cycle last in adults?
114080.e: A cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep lasts around 90 minutes. Then the next cycle begins.
114080.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

114081.q: Roughly how many sleep cycles do you go through in a normal night?
114081.e: With around 7 to 9 hours of sleep and about 90 minutes per cycle, that makes about 4 to 6 cycles. Each cycle is made up a little differently.
114081.m: In one night, the sleep cycles repeat four to six times.

114082.q: Into which two main types is sleep divided?
114082.e: A distinction is made between REM sleep with rapid eye movements and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep includes the falling-asleep phase, light sleep and deep sleep.
114082.m: Sleep consists of REM sleep and non-REM sleep.

114083.q: How long do healthy people usually take to fall asleep?
a: A few minutes to about half an hour
114083.e: The time from turning off the light to falling asleep is called sleep latency. In healthy people it is usually only a few minutes to about half an hour.
114083.m: Healthy people usually fall asleep within half an hour.

114084.q: Which sleep phase takes up the largest part of the night in adults?
114084.e: Light sleep makes up about half of all sleeping time. It occurs in every sleep cycle.
114084.m: We spend about half the night in light sleep.

114085.q: How can a sleep laboratory tell which sleep phase someone is in?
114085.e: Each sleep phase has typical patterns in the brain waves. In light sleep, for example, you see short bursts of waves called sleep spindles.
114085.m: The brain waves reveal the sleep phase.

114086.q: Roughly what does the curve of the sleep phases of one night look like?
a: Like a staircase that goes up and down several times
114086.e: During the night you switch several times between light sleep, deep sleep and dream sleep. The curve showing this is called a hypnogram and looks like a staircase.
114086.m: The sleep phases alternate several times during the night.

114087.q: What is the sudden jerk of the body just as you fall asleep called?
114087.e: A hypnic jerk is a harmless, short twitch of the muscles in the falling-asleep phase. It often feels as if you are falling.
114087.m: A jerk while falling asleep is usually harmless.

114088.q: In which sleep stage are you easiest to wake up?
a: In the first deep sleep phase
114088.e: The falling-asleep phase N1 is the transition from being awake to sleep. Even quiet noises can wake you up again then.
114088.m: You wake up most easily in the falling-asleep phase.

114089.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the internal clock that controls sleeping and waking last?
114089.e: The internal clock runs on a rhythm of about 24 hours. Experts call it circadian, from the Latin “circa dies”, about a day.
114089.m: The internal clock ticks on a daily rhythm.

114090.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and dream sleep last?
114090.e: In one night you go through several sleep cycles of about 90 minutes each. Such rhythms, which are shorter than a day, repeat several times.
114090.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

114091.q: Which rhythm only repeats once a year?
114091.e: Some rhythms last much longer than a day. Hibernation or bird migration repeat every year.

114092.q: Which hormone makes us tired in the evening?
114092.e: When it gets dark, the body produces more melatonin. It signals to the internal clock that it is time to sleep.

114093.q: Which bird are people compared to who like getting up early and get tired early?
114093.e: Early risers are called “larks” and night people “owls”. These types are called chronotypes and are partly inborn.
114093.m: Early risers are larks, night people are owls.

114094.q: How does the internal clock shift in many teenagers?
a: They get tired later in the evening
They get tired as early as the afternoon
They no longer need any sleep
They wake up at 4 in the morning
114094.e: In adolescence, the sleep-wake rhythm shifts later. Many teenagers only get tired late and find it hard to get up in the morning.
114094.m: Teenagers often only get tired late in the evening.

114095.q: What does science say about the biorhythm theory of fixed cycles of 23, 28 and 33 days from birth?
114095.e: This theory claims that body, feelings and mind follow fixed cycles from birth. Studies could not confirm this; it is considered a pseudoscience.
114095.m: Fixed biorhythm curves from birth are not scientifically proven.

114096.q: When during the day is a person’s body temperature at its lowest?
a: In the early hours of the morning
114096.e: Body temperature varies by just under one degree over the course of the day. It reaches its lowest point in the second half of the night, usually a few hours before waking.
114096.m: The body is coolest in the early hours of the morning.

114097.q: Where in the body is the main control of the internal clock?
114097.e: The master clock is a tiny area deep in the brain. It lies directly above the place where the optic nerves cross.
114097.m: The body’s master clock is in the brain.

114098.q: Through which sense organ does the internal clock find out whether it is day or night?
114098.e: Special cells in the retina report the brightness directly to the master clock in the brain through their own nerve pathway. That is why even some blind people still set their internal clock by light.
114098.m: The eyes tell the internal clock how bright it is.

114099.q: When does the body produce a particularly large amount of the sleep hormone melatonin?
a: At night, when it is dark
114099.e: Melatonin is mainly produced in the dark and makes us tired. Bright light, including from screens, slows down its production.
114099.m: In the dark, the body produces the sleep hormone melatonin.

114100.q: Which time cue sets the internal clock most strongly?
114100.e: Light is the body’s most important timekeeper. Every day it resets the internal clock to the change between day and night.

114101.q: How long does the internal clock’s day usually last in humans when there are no time cues?
114101.e: Without daylight and clocks, the internal clock in most people runs a little longer than 24 hours. That is why it has to be reset by light every day.
114101.m: The internal clock usually runs a bit slower than a 24-hour day.

a: A timekeeper in the body for the daily rhythm
A bone in the inner ear
An alarm clock in the bedroom
114102.e: The internal clock controls when we are tired or awake, when we are hungry and how warm our body is. It runs on a rhythm of about 24 hours.
114102.m: The internal clock controls our daily rhythm.

114103.q: What was found in people who lived for weeks without daylight or clocks in a bunker?
a: They kept sleeping and waking regularly
114103.e: In bunker experiments, people kept a sleep-wake rhythm of a little more than 24 hours. This proved that we have our own internal clock.
114103.m: Bunker experiments proved that humans have their own internal clock.

114104.q: Do plants have an internal clock too?
a: Yes, some open and close their leaves on a daily rhythm
No, only animals with a brain have one
114104.e: A mimosa kept in a dark cupboard still kept opening and closing its leaves on a daily rhythm. That is how it was discovered that plants also have an internal clock.
114104.m: Plants also have an internal clock.

114105.q: Which hormone rises sharply in the morning and helps us wake up?
114105.e: Cortisol reaches its peak shortly after waking up. It provides energy and gets the body going.
114105.m: In the morning, the hormone cortisol wakes us up.

114106.q: How many hours of sleep per night do experts recommend for teenagers aged 13 to 18?
114106.e: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep for teenagers. Many teenagers sleep much less on school days.
114106.m: Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

114107.q: What is the short, unintended nodding off called that is dangerous when driving, for example?
114107.e: In a microsleep, you fall asleep for a few seconds without noticing. At 100 km/h, a car travels more than 80 metres in three seconds.
114107.m: Microsleep at the wheel is life-threatening.

114108.q: How does lack of sleep typically affect appetite?
a: You are not hungry at all
114108.e: With lack of sleep, the hunger hormone ghrelin rises and the fullness hormone leptin falls. That is why people often eat more after short nights.
114108.m: People who sleep too little are often hungrier.

114109.q: What happens when a person does not sleep for several days?
a: Concentration and memory get much worse
114109.e: In 1964, a school pupil stayed awake for eleven days. Towards the end, he had great difficulty with concentration, memory and speech.
114109.m: Long sleep deprivation badly weakens concentration and memory.

114110.q: Studies compare performance after about 17 hours without sleep with which state?
a: With about 0.5 per mille alcohol in the blood
114110.e: Studies showed that reactions after about 17 hours awake are about as slow as with 0.5 per mille of alcohol. That is why tiredness is dangerous on the roads.
114110.m: Tiredness has a similar effect to alcohol.

114111.q: Which defence system of the body is weakened by constant lack of sleep?
114111.e: People who constantly sleep too little fall ill more easily. During sleep, the immune system works particularly hard.
114111.m: Enough sleep strengthens the body’s defences.

114112.q: What is the accumulated lack of sleep after several nights that are too short called?
114112.e: Missing hours of sleep add up to a sleep debt. It can only partly be made up by having a lie-in at the weekend.
114112.m: Missing sleep builds up as sleep debt.

114113.q: Which ability at school suffers most from too little sleep?
114113.e: After nights that are too short, it is hard to stay attentive and learn new things. Well-rested pupils learn more easily.
114113.m: When well rested, you can concentrate better.

114114.q: What problem do people with insomnia have?
a: They find it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep
They suddenly fall asleep during the day
114114.e: With insomnia, people lie awake for a long time or keep waking up during the night.
114114.m: Insomnia means having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.

114115.q: What are the rules and habits that encourage good sleep called?
114115.e: Sleep hygiene includes, for example, regular sleeping times, a dark, quiet room and no caffeine in the evening.
114115.m: Good sleep hygiene helps you fall asleep.

114116.q: Why does coffee keep you awake?
a: Caffeine blocks a tiredness substance in the brain
Coffee contains a great deal of sugar
114116.e: While you are awake, the substance adenosine builds up in the brain and makes you tired. Caffeine blocks its docking sites and so keeps you awake.
114116.m: Caffeine blocks tiredness in the brain.

114117.q: What do experts advise if you have not fallen asleep after about 20 minutes in bed?
a: Get up and do something calm
Do sport until you are exhausted
114117.e: You should not link your bed with lying awake and brooding. So you get up briefly, do something calm and only go back to bed when you are tired.
114117.m: If you cannot fall asleep, it is better to get up for a while.

114118.q: What helps most with long-lasting insomnia?
a: A therapy that changes sleeping habits
Lots of coffee in the morning
114118.e: Experts first recommend a therapy that changes unhelpful habits and thoughts about sleep. It is called cognitive behavioural therapy.
114118.m: Better sleeping habits help against long-lasting insomnia.

a: When the sleep problems go on for months
When you go to bed late once
When you have a lie-in at the weekend
114119.e: Chronic means long-lasting. Insomnia is called chronic when the problems occur several times a week for at least three months.

114120.q: What risk do many sleeping pills have when taken for a long time?
114120.e: Some sleeping pills lose their effect over time and can lead to dependence. They should therefore only be taken for a short time and after talking to a doctor.
114120.m: Sleeping pills should only be taken briefly and on medical advice.

114121.q: What kind of thoughts keep many people with insomnia awake at night?
114121.e: Stress and thoughts going round in circles are among the most common causes of problems falling asleep. Relaxation exercises or writing down your worries can help.
114121.m: Brooding in bed makes it harder to fall asleep.

a: Travelling quickly across several time zones
Sitting on a train for too long
Eating too much on the plane
114122.e: If you fly quickly across several time zones, the time at your destination no longer matches your internal clock. The body then needs a few days to adjust.
114122.m: Jet lag happens when the internal clock and local time do not match.

114123.q: In which direction of flight is jet lag worse for most people?
114123.e: When flying east, the day becomes shorter and you have to sleep earlier. This is harder for the internal clock than a longer day when flying west.
114123.m: Flights east usually cause the worse jet lag.

114124.q: According to a rule of thumb, roughly how much can the internal clock adjust per day?
114124.e: As a rule of thumb, it is around one time zone per day. After a flight across six time zones, you need about six days to adjust completely.
114124.m: The internal clock only shifts by about one hour per day.

114125.q: What is the usual time difference between Zurich and New York?
114125.e: When it is 6 pm in Zurich, it is usually only 12 noon in New York. Only for a few weeks a year, when the clocks change on different dates, is the difference 5 hours.
114125.m: New York is usually six hours behind Zurich.

114126.q: What helps most after arrival to get over jet lag faster?
a: Getting plenty of daylight at your destination
Sleeping all day in the hotel
114126.e: Daylight is the internal clock’s most important time cue. If you spend time outdoors during the day at your destination, you adjust faster.
114126.m: Daylight at your destination helps against jet lag.

114127.q: Why is it already evening in Tokyo when it is midday in Zurich?
a: Tokyo is further east, where the sun rises earlier
All the clocks in Japan are wrong
Tokyo is in the southern hemisphere
Japan is closer to the sun
114127.e: The Earth turns from west to east. That is why the day starts earlier in the east, and Tokyo is several hours ahead of Switzerland.
114127.m: In the east, the day starts earlier.

114128.q: Why do you hardly get jet lag after a flight from Zurich to Johannesburg?
a: Both are almost in the same time zone
There is no clock time in Africa
114128.e: Johannesburg lies south of Zurich and has at most one hour’s time difference. The flight is long, but the internal clock hardly has to adjust.
114128.m: North-south flights cause hardly any jet lag.

114129.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of jet lag?
a: Tiredness during the day and lying awake at night
114129.e: With jet lag, you are tired or wide awake at the wrong time of day. Problems with concentration and digestion are often added.
114129.m: Jet lag makes you tired by day and awake at night.

114130.q: Which colour of light does the internal clock react to most strongly?
114130.e: In the eye there are sensory cells that react particularly to blue light. They tell the brain that it is daytime. Red light has hardly any effect on the internal clock.
114130.m: The internal clock reacts most strongly to blue light.

114131.q: What colour are the lenses of glasses that are meant to filter out blue light in the evening, usually?
114131.e: Yellow and orange lenses absorb a large part of the blue light. Blue or violet lenses, on the other hand, would let exactly this light through.
114131.m: Blue light filter glasses usually have yellowish or orange lenses.

114132.q: Which light sources give off a particularly large amount of blue light in the evening?
114132.e: The white LEDs in screens have a high proportion of blue. Candles and fire, on the other hand, glow yellowish-red with little blue.
114132.m: Phone screens give off a lot of blue light.

114133.q: What does the night mode on many phones do to the screen colour?
a: It makes it warmer and more yellowish
It makes it black and white
114133.e: Night mode reduces the proportion of blue and gives the picture a yellowish tint. But the most effective thing is to put the screen away completely before sleeping.
114133.m: Night mode makes the screen more yellowish.

114134.q: What does the kelvin figure on a light bulb packet show?
a: Whether the light looks warm or cold
How much electricity the bulb uses
114134.e: Warm white light has about 2,700 kelvin, cold daylight white over 5,000 kelvin. The higher the value, the more blue the light contains.
114134.m: The kelvin number shows the light colour of a bulb.

114135.q: Which lamp is better suited to the bedroom in the evening?
114135.e: Warm white light contains little blue and disturbs melatonin production less. This makes it easier to fall asleep.
114135.m: In the evening, warm, dimmed light is best.

114136.q: How long before sleeping do experts often recommend putting screens away?
114136.e: Light and exciting content keep the brain awake. That is why people are often advised not to use screens for about an hour before sleeping.
114136.m: An hour without screens before sleeping encourages good sleep.

114137.q: When is bright light rich in blue actually helpful for the internal clock?
a: In the middle of the night
114137.e: Bright light in the morning stops melatonin production and wakes you up. It sets the internal clock to an early start to the day.
114137.m: Bright light in the morning wakes you up.

114138.q: Roughly how long should a power nap last?
114138.e: A short sleep of 10 to 20 minutes refreshes you without falling into deep sleep. Afterwards you are quickly fit again.
114138.m: A power nap lasts no more than about 20 minutes.

114139.q: Why should a power nap not last much longer than 20 to 30 minutes?
a: Otherwise you go into deep sleep
114139.e: After about half an hour, deep sleep often begins. If you wake up from it, you feel worse instead of rested.
114139.m: A nap that is too long tends to make you more tired.

114140.q: At what time of day is a power nap best?
114140.e: After midday there is a natural dip in performance. A short sleep at this time disturbs night-time sleep the least.
114140.m: The after-lunch dip is a good time for a nap.

114141.q: What is the traditional midday rest in Spain called?
114141.e: The word siesta comes from the Latin “sexta hora”, the sixth hour after sunrise. It refers to midday.
114141.m: In Spain, the siesta is the midday rest.

114142.q: What helps to stop a power nap from getting too long?
114142.e: With an alarm set for about 20 minutes, you wake up before deep sleep begins. That way you feel fresh afterwards.
114142.m: An alarm keeps the power nap short.

114143.q: In which professional group did NASA study the effect of a short sleep of around 26 minutes in 1995?
114143.e: In the NASA study, pilots on long-haul flights slept briefly in the cockpit. Afterwards they were much more alert and reacted faster.
114143.m: A short sleep clearly increases alertness.

114144.q: What is a short sleep during the day called?
114144.e: A nap is a short, light sleep, often after lunch. The expression power nap emphasises its refreshing effect.
114144.m: A nap is a short sleep during the day.

114145.q: What helps to stop a short nap during the day from lasting too long?
114145.e: An alarm makes sure you wake up again after 10 to 20 minutes. That way the nap stays short and refreshing.
114145.m: An alarm keeps the nap short.

114146.q: What happens during an examination in a sleep laboratory?
a: Many body readings are measured at the same time during sleep
You learn to read faster on a course
114146.e: In the sleep laboratory, brain waves, eye movements, muscle tension, breathing and heartbeat are recorded, among other things. This makes it possible to detect sleep disorders.
114146.m: In the sleep laboratory, many readings are measured during sleep.

114147.q: How are brain waves measured in the sleep laboratory?
114147.e: Electrodes on the scalp measure the electrical activity of the brain. This measurement is called an EEG. It shows the sleep phases.
114147.m: Electrodes on the head measure brain waves.

114148.q: Why are eye movements also measured in the sleep laboratory?
a: Because they move quickly during dream sleep
To test how sharp your eyesight is
To find out your eye colour
Because otherwise the eyes dry out
114148.e: In REM sleep, when we dream a lot, the eyes move quickly back and forth. Electrodes next to the eyes record this.
114148.m: Rapid eye movements show dream sleep.

114149.q: What is measured in the sleep laboratory with electrodes on the chin and legs?
114149.e: Electrodes on the skin record the tension of the muscles. In REM sleep, muscle tension is very low.
114149.m: Electrodes on the chin and legs show how hard the muscles are working.

a: Breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep
You grind your teeth at night
You suddenly fall asleep during the day
114150.e: In sleep apnoea, breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep. People affected often snore loudly and are very tired during the day.
114150.m: In sleep apnoea, breathing stops during sleep.

114151.q: Which device is often used against sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure
114151.e: In CPAP therapy, a machine gently blows air into the airways through a mask. This keeps them open and the pauses in breathing disappear.
114151.m: A positive pressure mask keeps the airways open in sleep apnoea.

114152.q: What does a pulse oximeter on the finger measure during the night?
a: The oxygen saturation of the blood
114152.e: The pulse oximeter shines light through the finger and works out how much oxygen the blood is carrying. When breathing stops, this value falls.
114152.m: A pulse oximeter measures the oxygen in the blood.

114153.q: What happens in the illness narcolepsy?
a: You suddenly fall asleep during the day without wanting to
You cannot fall asleep at all at night
114153.e: People with narcolepsy have a disturbed control of sleeping and waking. They can fall asleep in the middle of everyday situations.
114153.m: With narcolepsy, sleep suddenly overwhelms you.

114154.q: Why did Switzerland introduce summer time?
a: To have the same time as its neighbouring countries
So that the cows would give more milk
114154.e: When the neighbouring countries had summer time and Switzerland did not, there were problems with train timetables and trade. That is why Switzerland has also had summer time since 1981.
114154.m: With summer time, Switzerland fell into line with its neighbours.

114155.q: What was Switzerland called in the summer of 1980 because it was the only country around without summer time?
114155.e: All the neighbouring countries had summer time in 1980, but Switzerland did not. This caused problems, for example with train timetables and trade.
114155.m: In 1980, Switzerland was a time island in Europe.

114156.q: On which day does summer time begin in Switzerland?
a: On the last Sunday in March
On the first Sunday in May
On the last Sunday in February
114156.e: On the last Sunday in March, the clock is put forward from 2 am to 3 am. Switzerland follows the EU rules on this.
114156.m: Summer time begins on the last Sunday in March.

114157.q: What happens to the length of your sleep on the night summer time begins?
a: The length of sleep stays the same
114157.e: The clock jumps from 2 am straight to 3 am. If you get up at the usual time, you have slept an hour less.
114157.m: In spring, the clock change costs you an hour of sleep.

114158.q: What is the standard time that applies in Switzerland in winter called?
114158.e: Central European Time (CET) is one hour ahead of universal time UTC. In summer, Central European Summer Time applies, two hours ahead.
114158.m: In winter, Central European Time applies in Switzerland.

114159.q: When was summer time first introduced in Europe?
114159.e: In 1916, in the middle of the First World War, Germany and Austria-Hungary introduced summer time. They wanted to save energy for lighting.
114159.m: Summer time has existed since the First World War.

114160.q: What was the original aim of summer time?
a: To make better use of daylight and save energy
To make the school holidays longer
114160.e: Putting the clock forward means it stays light for longer in the evening. This was supposed to mean less artificial light was needed. Today, however, the actual saving is disputed.
114160.m: Summer time was meant to help make better use of daylight.

114161.q: Which way do you turn the clock in spring when the clocks change?
114161.e: A well-known memory aid is “spring forward, fall back”. So in spring you put the clock forward, and in autumn you put it back.
114161.m: In spring you put the clock forward, in autumn back.

114163.q: Roughly how efficient are today's standard commercial solar panels?
114163.e: Common silicon panels turn around a fifth of the incoming light energy into electricity. The rest mainly becomes heat or is reflected.
114163.m: Solar panels use about a fifth of sunlight.

114164.q: What material are most solar cells made of?
114164.e: Silicon is obtained from quartz sand. It is the most important material for solar cells and also for computer chips.
114164.m: Most solar cells are made of silicon.

114165.q: Which unit is used to give the peak power of a solar installation?
114165.e: Kilowatt peak means the power under standard test conditions with strong sunshine. In everyday use the installation usually supplies less.
114165.m: The peak power of a solar installation is measured in kilowatt peak.

114166.q: Which device in a solar installation converts the panels' direct current into alternating current for the household grid?
114166.e: Solar cells supply direct current, but the power grid works with alternating current. The inverter adapts the current accordingly.
114166.m: The inverter turns direct current into alternating current.

114167.q: What is it called when a household directly uses the electricity from its own solar installation?
114167.e: Electricity you use yourself doesn't have to be bought expensively from the grid. So high self-consumption pays off, for example if the washing machine runs at midday.
114167.m: Solar electricity you use yourself is called self-consumption.

114168.q: Why do solar installations in the Alps produce more electricity in winter than in the Swiss Plateau?
a: They are often above the fog, and snow reflects light
The Sun shines there at night
It is warmer in the mountains
The days there are longer in winter
114168.e: In winter the Swiss Plateau often lies under a blanket of high fog, while it is sunny in the mountains. Snow also throws extra light onto the panels, and cold improves their efficiency.
114168.m: Alpine solar installations are especially valuable in winter.

114169.q: A solar installation has 10 kWp and produces around 1000 kWh per kWp a year. Roughly how much electricity does it produce per year?
114169.e: You work out 10 kWp times 1000 kWh per kWp. That makes 10,000 kWh a year.
114169.m: The yearly yield is the installation's power times the yield per kilowatt peak.

114170.q: What is the main difference between solar thermal and photovoltaics?
a: Solar thermal produces heat, photovoltaics electricity
Solar thermal only works at night
114170.e: Solar thermal installations use sunlight to warm a liquid, for example for hot water or heating. Photovoltaics, on the other hand, produces electric current.
114170.m: Solar thermal gives heat, photovoltaics gives electricity.

114171.q: What is the part on the roof called that captures the Sun's heat in solar thermal systems?
114171.e: A solar collector contains a dark absorber that turns radiation into heat. A liquid carries this heat into the house.
114171.m: Solar collectors capture the Sun's heat.

114172.q: What is the vacuum in an evacuated tube collector for?
114172.e: In a vacuum there is no air that could carry heat away. That is why evacuated tubes work well even in the cold.
114172.m: A vacuum insulates especially well against heat loss.

114173.q: Why is glycol added to the water in many solar collectors?
a: So that it doesn't freeze in winter
114173.e: Glycol lowers the freezing point of the liquid. So the pipes on the roof don't burst even in frost.
114173.m: Glycol protects solar collectors from frost.

114174.q: Why are the absorbers of solar collectors coloured dark?
a: Dark surfaces absorb the most light
So that they don't look dirty
114174.e: Dark surfaces absorb almost all the light and turn it into heat. Light-coloured surfaces would reflect a lot of light.
114174.m: Dark surfaces get warmest in the sun.

114175.q: Where is the water heated by the Sun stored in the house?
114175.e: A well-insulated hot water tank, often called a boiler in Switzerland, keeps the water warm for hours. So warm water is still available in the evening.
114175.m: A hot water tank stores the warm water.

114176.q: What is a power station called in which many mirrors focus sunlight onto the top of a tall tower?
114176.e: The mirrors concentrate the light so strongly that very high temperatures arise in the tower. This produces steam, which drives a turbine.
114176.m: In a solar tower power station, mirrors focus sunlight onto a tower.

114177.q: What is solar thermal energy most often used for in Swiss detached houses?
114177.e: In detached houses, solar collectors often cover a large part of the hot water needed. Some systems also help with the heating.
114177.m: Solar thermal energy mainly supplies hot water.

114178.q: Which form of the wind's energy does a wind turbine use?
114178.e: The moving air turns the rotor, and a generator turns this into electricity. In physics the energy of movement is called kinetic energy.
114178.m: Wind turbines turn kinetic energy into electricity.

114179.q: How many rotor blades do most modern wind turbines have?
114179.e: Three blades are a good compromise between output, smooth running and the amount of material. That is why almost all large turbines have three rotor blades.
114179.m: Modern wind turbines usually have three rotor blades.

114180.q: The power of the wind grows with the cube of the wind speed. How many times greater is it at double the wind speed?
114180.e: You work out 2 cubed, so 2 times 2 times 2. That makes 8. That is why windy sites are so important.
114180.m: Twice as much wind brings eight times as much power.

114181.q: Can a wind turbine use all the energy of the wind?
a: No, the wind must keep flowing behind the rotor
Yes, good turbines use all of it
Yes, but only in a storm
No, wind turbines use no wind energy at all
114181.e: If a wind turbine took all the energy from the wind, the air behind the rotor would stand still and no more wind would follow. So it can only use part of it, at most about 59 per cent.
114181.m: No wind turbine can use all the energy of the wind.

114182.q: On which Swiss Alpine pass did a wind farm with five turbines start operating in 2020?
114182.e: The Gotthard wind farm stands at around 2100 metres above sea level near the Gotthard Hospice. It is one of the highest wind farms in Europe.
114182.m: Wind turbines have been turning on the Gotthard Pass since 2020.

114183.q: Why are many wind farms built at sea (offshore)?
a: The wind there is stronger and steadier
114183.e: Over the open sea there are no hills or forests to slow the wind. So offshore turbines produce more electricity, but are more expensive to build.
114183.m: At sea the wind blows more strongly and steadily.

114184.q: Roughly how high is the hub of large modern wind turbines on land?
114184.e: Modern turbines often have hub heights of over 100 metres. Higher up, the wind blows more strongly and steadily than near the ground.
114184.m: The higher a wind turbine, the more wind it catches.

114185.q: What does a wind turbine do in a very strong storm?
a: It switches itself off for protection
It turns as fast as possible
114185.e: Above a certain wind speed, the blades are turned out of the wind and the rotor is stopped. This protects the turbine from damage.
114185.m: In a storm, wind turbines switch off.

114186.q: What is an important disadvantage of wind power?
a: It uses a lot of oil
114186.e: When there is no wind the turbines stand still; when it is windy they produce a lot of electricity. So storage and other power stations are needed to balance this out.
114186.m: Wind power varies with the weather.

114187.q: Apart from methane, which gas is the second largest part of biogas?
114187.e: As well as methane, biogas contains a lot of carbon dioxide, which does not burn. It is removed before the gas is fed into the gas network.
114187.m: As well as methane, biogas contains a lot of carbon dioxide.

114188.q: Under what condition do bacteria break down the material in a biogas plant?
