116432.m: The UV index measures radiation that causes sunburn.

116433.q: Why is a single UVB photon more dangerous for DNA than a UVA photon?
a: It carries more energy because of its shorter wavelength
It only has an effect at night
116433.e: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength. The more energetic UVB photons are also absorbed right in the range where DNA absorbs light.
116433.m: The shorter the wavelength, the more energetic the photon.

116434.q: Which skin cancer is the most common type of cancer of all in people with fair skin?
116434.e: Basal cell carcinoma, also called basalioma, is the most common malignant tumour in people with fair skin. It usually grows slowly.
116434.m: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in people with fair skin.

116435.q: What is typical of the way a basal cell carcinoma grows?
a: It destroys locally but rarely forms metastases
It spreads to the lungs very early
It grows only in mucous membranes
116435.e: Basal cell carcinoma can destroy surrounding tissue down to the bone. However, it only very rarely forms secondary tumours, which is why it is sometimes called semi-malignant.
116435.m: A basalioma grows destructively but hardly spreads.

116436.q: On which part of the body do basal cell carcinomas occur most often?
116436.e: Most basaliomas develop in places that get a lot of sun over decades, especially the face. The nose, forehead and ears are typical.
116436.m: Basaliomas usually develop on the sun-exposed face.

116437.q: What does a nodular basal cell carcinoma typically look like?
a: A glassy lump with a pearly edge and fine little blood vessels
A black spot with a ragged edge
116437.e: Typical are a skin-coloured to reddish, glassy shiny lump and a raised edge like a string of pearls. Widened blood vessels are often visible on the surface.
116437.m: A basalioma often shows a pearly raised edge.

116438.q: Which kind of UV exposure is considered the most important risk factor for basal cell carcinoma?
a: The UV dose built up over a lifetime
116438.e: The risk rises with the UV dose added up over a lifetime. That is why older people and people who work outdoors a lot are especially affected.
116438.m: For basalioma, the total UV dose of a lifetime counts.

116439.q: What does UV radiation do in skin cells that can lead to skin cancer such as basal cell carcinoma?
a: It fills the cells with water
It uses up all the melanin
116439.e: UV radiation changes building blocks of DNA. If the damage is not repaired, mutations arise and a cell can divide uncontrollably.
116439.m: Skin cancer is caused by UV damage to DNA.

116440.q: What is the standard treatment for a basal cell carcinoma?
116440.e: The basalioma is usually cut out completely. Microscopic examination of the cut edges checks whether the tumour has been fully removed.

116441.q: Why are the cut edges examined under the microscope after a basal cell carcinoma has been cut out?
a: To check whether the tumour has been completely removed
To count bacteria in the wound
116441.e: If tumour cells remain at the edge, the cancer can grow back. That is why more is cut away until the edges are free of tumour.
116441.m: Tumour-free edges show that the cancer has been completely removed.

116442.q: Why is a melanoma that grows quickly downwards particularly dangerous?
a: It quickly reaches blood and lymph vessels
It grows only on the scalp
It can never be operated on
116442.e: Blood and lymph vessels lie in the deeper dermis. The deeper a melanoma reaches, the more easily tumour cells can travel through them to other organs.
116442.m: The deeper a melanoma grows, the more dangerous it is.

116443.q: What does the “E” stand for in the ABCDE rule for assessing moles?
116443.e: The rule checks asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolution. A mole that changes in size, shape or colour should be examined by a doctor.
116443.m: A mole that changes should be checked by a doctor.

116444.q: From which cells does a melanoma develop?
a: From the pigment cells of the skin
From the fat cells of the subcutis
116444.e: A melanoma is a malignant tumour of the melanocytes, the cells that make the pigment melanin. That is why it is often dark in colour.
116444.m: A melanoma is a tumour of the pigment cells.

116445.q: Why is melanoma also called “black skin cancer” in German?
a: Because it is usually darkly pigmented
Because it occurs only on dark skin
Because it grows mainly at night
116445.e: Melanomas develop from pigment cells and often make a lot of melanin. That is why they usually look brown to black, unlike the light-coloured skin cancers.
116445.m: Melanomas are usually dark because they develop from pigment cells.

116446.q: Why should you also check the soles of your feet and your nails for unusual dark spots?
a: Melanomas can also develop in places that get little sun
There are no pigment cells there
The skin there is immune to cancer
116446.e: Not every melanoma is caused by the sun. One form grows on the palms, soles or under the nails, and in people with dark skin it is even the most common.
116446.m: Melanomas can also develop on the soles of the feet and under the nails.

116447.q: What lies behind the development of a melanoma at the level of the cell?
a: Changes in the DNA of the pigment cells
Too much melanin in the blood
116447.e: UV radiation can damage the DNA of pigment cells. If such mutations build up, for example in the BRAF gene, the cells divide uncontrollably.
116447.m: Melanomas are caused by DNA damage, often from UV radiation.

116448.q: Which treatment has greatly improved the chances in melanoma that has spread since the 2010s?
a: Immunotherapies that activate the immune system against the tumour
116448.e: New immunotherapies release a brake on the immune system. This allows T cells to attack the tumour cells more effectively.
116448.m: Immunotherapies help the immune system fight melanoma cells.

116449.q: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy for in melanoma?
a: To check whether tumour cells have spread into the lymph system
116449.e: The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node in the area that drains the tumour. If it is free of tumour cells, spread through the lymph is unlikely.
116449.m: The sentinel lymph node shows whether a melanoma has spread.

116450.q: Which factor raises the risk of melanoma particularly clearly?
a: Many moles and sunburns in childhood
Swimming often in an indoor pool
116450.e: A high number of moles and bad sunburns at a young age are among the most important risk factors. Fair skin and cases in the family also raise the risk.
116450.m: Sunburns in childhood raise the risk of melanoma.

116451.q: Which instrument do dermatologists use to examine moles magnified and lit up?
116451.e: The dermatoscope works with magnification and incident light. This makes structures in the skin visible that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
116451.m: With a dermatoscope you can see moles more closely.

116452.q: What does the “ugly duckling sign” mean when checking the skin?
a: A mole that looks different from all the others is suspicious
Moles on the hands are harmless
116452.e: Most of a person's moles look alike. A mole that does not fit the pattern, an ugly duckling, should be examined more closely.
116452.m: A mole that stands out from the rest should be checked.

116453.q: Which form of prevention does early detection of skin cancer belong to?
116453.e: Early detection means finding a disease that has already developed as early as possible. At this stage it can usually be treated well.

116454.q: Which measure belongs to the primary prevention of skin cancer?
a: Protection with clothing, a hat and shade
116454.e: Primary prevention aims to stop a disease from developing at all. For skin cancer this mainly means reducing UV exposure.
116454.m: The best protection against skin cancer is less UV radiation.

a: Specialists assessing skin images from a distance
Treating the skin with television light
A skin check only by phone without images
Measuring skin temperature from a distance
116455.e: In teledermatology, photos or dermatoscope images are sent electronically to specialists. They can then judge whether an examination in person is needed.
116455.m: Teledermatology assesses skin images from a distance.

116456.q: Which simple shadow rule helps you recognise the time of high UV exposure?
a: If your shadow is shorter than you are, look for shade
If your shadow is longer than you are, put on cream
Without a shadow there is no UV radiation
116456.e: A short shadow means the sun is high. Then the path through the atmosphere is short and UV radiation is correspondingly strong.
116456.m: A short shadow warns of strong UV radiation.

116457.q: After removal, how is a suspicious skin finding reliably confirmed or ruled out as cancer?
116457.e: The removed tissue is examined under the microscope in histology. Only this finding gives a confirmed diagnosis.
116457.m: Histology confirms the diagnosis of skin cancer.

116458.q: Why is a mirror or a second person useful when checking your own skin?
a: Because the back and scalp are otherwise hard to see
Because moles look bigger in the mirror
Because light would otherwise change the moles
Because it shows your blood group
116458.e: Skin cancer can develop anywhere, including places that are hard to see. With a mirror or help, you can check your back, neck and scalp.
116458.m: Self-checks should include places that are hard to see.

116459.q: Why should an actinic keratosis be treated?
a: It can develop into skin cancer
116459.e: Actinic keratoses are precancerous lesions. Without treatment they can turn into a light-coloured skin cancer.
116459.m: An actinic keratosis is a precancerous lesion.

116460.q: How does an actinic keratosis typically feel?
116460.e: The patches are often scaly and horny. They can often be felt better than seen.

116461.q: Where do actinic keratoses occur particularly often?
a: On a bald head, the forehead and the backs of the hands
On the soles of the feet
116461.e: The changes develop where the skin gets a lot of UV radiation over years. Typical places are a hairless scalp, the face, ears and the backs of the hands.
116461.m: Actinic keratoses grow in places plagued by the sun.

116462.q: What is the main trigger of actinic keratoses?
a: Chronic UV exposure over many years
A virus from the swimming pool
116462.e: The word actinic means caused by radiation. Years of sun exposure damage the DNA of the keratinocytes.
116462.m: Actinic keratoses are the result of years of sun exposure.

116463.q: Which treatment is often used for single actinic keratoses?
116463.e: In cryotherapy the patch is frozen with liquid nitrogen. The damaged cells die and healthy skin grows back.
116463.m: Single keratoses can be frozen off.

116464.q: What does the term “field cancerisation” mean for actinic keratoses?
a: The whole sun-damaged area of skin is altered
The cancer only grows on fields
Only one single spot is affected
116464.e: Besides the visible patches, the whole surrounding skin is often already UV-damaged. That is why whole areas are often treated instead of just single spots.
116464.m: In field cancerisation a whole area of skin is damaged.

116465.q: How does photodynamic therapy work for actinic keratoses?
a: An applied substance makes diseased cells sensitive to light, and light destroys them
UVB light turns the keratoses brown
116465.e: A cream with aminolevulinic acid builds up in the altered cells. When light is shone on them, reactive oxygen compounds form that kill these cells.
116465.m: In photodynamic therapy, light destroys marked precancerous cells.

116466.q: Which occupational group has a particularly high risk of actinic keratoses?
a: People who work outdoors a lot
People who work in an office at night
People who work in a laboratory
116466.e: Anyone who works, for example, in construction, farming or as a mountain guide is exposed to strong sunlight for years. In Germany, multiple actinic keratoses and squamous cell carcinomas caused by UV radiation have therefore been recognised as an occupational disease since 2015.
116466.m: People who work outdoors need especially good sun protection.

116467.q: How do mineral UV filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide work?
a: They scatter, reflect and absorb UV radiation
116467.e: Mineral filters are fine particles that reflect, scatter and partly absorb UV radiation. They are considered well tolerated but can leave a white film.
116467.m: Mineral filters protect with tiny particles on the skin.

116468.q: What happens to the energy that organic UV filters absorb?
a: It is mostly given off as heat
It is converted into vitamin D
It is given off again as UVC
It is stored in the filter
116468.e: Organic filter molecules absorb UV photons and enter an excited state. When they fall back, they give off the energy mostly as heat.
116468.m: Organic UV filters turn UV energy into heat.

116469.q: How is the sun protection factor defined?
a: As the ratio of the sunburn threshold with and without sunscreen
As the share of infrared radiation blocked
As the number of hours of protection per application
As the amount of filter in grams per tube
116469.e: The SPF compares the UV dose that causes minimal redness with sunscreen to the dose without protection. An SPF of 20 means that about twenty times the dose is needed.
116469.m: The sun protection factor tells you how many times more UVB the skin can tolerate.

116470.q: Roughly what share of UVB radiation does a sunscreen with SPF 30 hold back when used correctly?
116470.e: With SPF 30, about one thirtieth of the radiation reaches the skin, so just over 3 per cent. About 97 per cent is blocked.

116471.q: Why do many people not reach the sun protection factor stated on the pack in everyday life?
a: They put on too little sun cream
They put cream on in the shade
116471.e: In the lab the sun protection factor is measured with 2 milligrams per square centimetre of skin. In everyday life most people only use a fraction of that, which clearly lowers the protection.
116471.m: If you apply too thinly, you do not get the stated protection.

116472.q: Does reapplying sunscreen on the same day extend the total protection time beyond the original?
a: No, it only maintains the protection
116472.e: Reapplying replaces sunscreen that has been rubbed or washed off. However, the maximum protection time, which comes from the skin's own protection time and the SPF, is not extended.
116472.m: Reapplying maintains protection but does not extend it.

116473.q: Which US state was the first to ban sunscreens with the filters oxybenzone and octinoxate to protect coral reefs?
116473.e: In 2018 Hawaii decided to ban the sale of sunscreens with these two filters. The ban came into force in 2021 because the substances might harm corals.
116473.m: Some UV filters are suspected of harming corals.

116474.q: Why is titanium dioxide often used as nanoparticles in sun creams?
a: Finer particles leave less of a white film
116474.e: Large pigment particles also scatter visible light and make the skin look white. Very small particles are almost transparent but still filter UV.
116474.m: Nanoparticles make mineral sun cream more transparent.

116475.q: In the EU, what is the highest permitted sun protection factor label on sunscreens?
116475.e: According to an EU recommendation, products with very high protection are labelled “50+”. Higher numbers would suggest an extra benefit that hardly exists.
116475.m: The highest sun protection factor on EU labels is 50+.

116476.q: What causes the immediate pigmentation shortly after UVA exposure?
a: Melanin already present is oxidised and darkens
Blood builds up in the skin
116476.e: In immediate pigmentation no new melanin is made. Existing pigment precursors are oxidised by UVA, and the colour usually fades again quickly.
116476.m: The immediate tan only darkens pigment that is already there.

116477.q: After how long does the delayed tan from newly formed melanin become visible?
116477.e: In delayed pigmentation the melanocytes make new melanin and pass it on to the keratinocytes. This process takes a few days.
116477.m: A real tan only develops after a few days.

116478.q: Roughly how much protection does a well-developed suntan give?
a: About the same as a sun protection factor of 2 to 4
About the same as a sun protection factor of 30
About the same as a sun protection factor of 50
116478.e: A tan offers only slight natural protection. It does not replace sun cream, clothing or shade.
116478.m: Tanned skin is only weakly protected against UV.

116479.q: From a biological point of view, what does a tan show?
a: A reaction to UV damage in the skin
116479.e: Tanning is triggered when UV radiation damages the DNA of keratinocytes. Through signalling substances these cells stimulate the melanocytes to make pigment.
116479.m: A tan is a sign that the skin is defending itself against damage.

116480.q: Which cells in the skin make the pigment melanin?
116480.e: Melanocytes sit in the lowest layer of the epidermis. They make melanin and pass it on to the surrounding skin cells, which become darker as a result.
116480.m: Melanocytes make the skin pigment melanin.

116481.q: Which active ingredient in self-tanners colours the horny layer without UV radiation?
116481.e: Dihydroxyacetone reacts with amino acids in the top layer of skin to form brown compounds. This colour does not protect against UV radiation and disappears as the skin flakes off.
116481.m: Self-tanners colour the skin but do not protect against the sun.

116482.q: Which rule applies in Switzerland to the use of sunbeds by minors?
a: It is only allowed with sun cream
It is only allowed in winter
116482.e: Under the Federal Act on Protection against Dangers from Non-Ionising Radiation and Sound, young people under 18 may not use sunbeds. Their skin is considered particularly sensitive.
116482.m: In Switzerland, sunbeds are banned for minors.

116483.q: Which fashion designer is considered to have made the suntan an ideal of beauty in the 1920s?
116483.e: Before that, pale skin was considered refined in Europe. Coco Chanel appeared with a tan, and a tan became a sign of leisure and wealth.
116483.m: A tan only became an ideal of beauty in the 20th century.

116484.q: Why is it useful to know your own skin type?
a: To calculate your vitamin C needs
116484.e: The skin type shows how sensitively the skin reacts to sun. If you know it, you can adapt sun cream, clothing and time in the sun better.
116484.m: Your skin type helps you choose the right sun protection.

116485.q: How many skin types does the Fitzpatrick scale distinguish?
116485.e: The scale ranges from type I with very fair skin that always burns to type VI with deeply dark skin. There are four more levels in between.
116485.m: The Fitzpatrick scale has six skin types.

116486.q: Which feature describes Fitzpatrick skin type I?
a: Always burns and practically never tans
116486.e: People with skin type I have very fair skin, often freckles and reddish hair. They have the shortest natural protection time.
116486.m: Skin type I burns quickly and hardly tans.

116487.q: By which criterion are Fitzpatrick skin types mainly classified?
a: By how the skin reacts to sun
By the fat content of the skin
By the number of hairs per cm²
116487.e: What matters is how easily the skin gets sunburnt and how well it tans. From this its sensitivity to light can be estimated.
116487.m: Skin types describe how sensitive the skin is to sun.

116488.q: What does the term “natural protection time” of the skin mean?
a: The time without protection until sunburn begins
The time until the skin grows back
The time until sun cream soaks in
The time until a tan fades
116488.e: The natural protection time tells you how long unprotected skin can be exposed to the sun before it turns red. It depends on skin type and the UV index.
116488.m: The natural protection time is especially short for fair skin.

116489.q: A person has a natural protection time of 10 minutes and uses SPF 30 correctly. What is the theoretical maximum protection time?
116489.e: You multiply the natural protection time by the sun protection factor: 10 minutes times 30 makes 300 minutes. Experts recommend using only about two thirds of this time.
116489.m: Protection time is natural protection time times sun protection factor.

116490.q: Which skin types are especially common among people in Switzerland of central European origin?
116490.e: Many people of central European origin have fair to medium-fair skin that first burns and then tans. This corresponds to skin types II and III.
116490.m: In central Europe, skin types II and III are most common.

116491.q: Can people with skin type VI get skin cancer?
116491.e: Dark skin is better protected against UV, but not completely. In dark skin, skin cancer is also often detected late, for example on the soles of the feet.
116491.m: Even very dark skin can develop skin cancer.

116492.q: Which group of cells do the Langerhans cells of the skin belong to?
a: Dendritic cells of the immune system
Muscle cells of the hair follicle muscles
116492.e: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting immune cells of the epidermis. With their extensions they form a dense surveillance network.
116492.m: Langerhans cells are the immune system's guards in the epidermis.

116493.q: What did Paul Langerhans first think the cells he discovered in the epidermis in 1868 were?
116493.e: Paul Langerhans described the branched cells in 1868 as a young medical student. Because of their extensions he thought they were nerve cells; their role in the immune system was only recognised about a hundred years later.
116493.m: Langerhans cells were first thought to be nerve cells.

116494.q: How do Langerhans cells keep watch over the whole epidermis even though there are only a few of them?
a: By forming a horny layer themselves
116494.e: Langerhans cells stretch their extensions out between the skin cells and so form a dense network. Under the electron microscope they can also be recognised by the tennis-racket-shaped Birbeck granules.
116494.m: Langerhans cells form a surveillance network with their extensions.

116495.q: What do Langerhans cells do after they have taken up a foreign antigen?
a: They travel to the lymph nodes and present it to T cells
They dissolve in the horny layer
116495.e: The cells process the antigen and travel through lymph vessels to the lymph nodes. There they activate T lymphocytes and start a targeted defence.
116495.m: Langerhans cells take foreign substances to the T cells.

116496.q: What effect does UV radiation have on Langerhans cells?
a: It reduces their number and function
It turns them into fat cells
116496.e: UV radiation weakens Langerhans cells and so suppresses the immune defence in the skin. This makes it easier for damaged cells to escape immune control.
116496.m: UV radiation weakens the skin's immune system.

116497.q: How are Langerhans cells made specifically visible in a skin sample under the microscope?
a: With labelled antibodies against their surface molecules
With a magnifying glass and no staining at all
116497.e: Langerhans cells carry typical molecules such as CD1a and langerin. Labelled antibodies bind to them and stain the cells specifically.
116497.m: Labelled antibodies are used to stain particular cells specifically.

116498.q: Which structures should Langerhans cells of the skin not be confused with, even though they have the same discoverer?
a: Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
116498.e: Paul Langerhans also described groups of cells in the pancreas that make hormones such as insulin. These have nothing to do with the immune cells of the skin.
116498.m: Langerhans cells and islets of Langerhans are different things.

116499.q: In which part of the skin are Langerhans cells mainly found?
a: In the bone marrow of the skin
116499.e: Langerhans cells sit mainly in the middle layers of the epidermis. There they catch pathogens and foreign substances that get past the horny layer.
116499.m: Langerhans cells keep watch over the epidermis.

116500.q: Which layer of skin forms the most important physical barrier against water loss?
116500.e: The horny layer consists of dead, keratinised cells embedded in lipids. It stops the body losing too much water.
116500.m: The horny layer is the skin's most important barrier.

116501.q: Which model gives a clear picture of how the horny layer is built?
116501.e: The keratinised cells are the bricks, the lipids between them the mortar. Together they make a tight wall.
116501.m: The horny layer is built like a wall of bricks and mortar.

116502.q: Which group of lipids makes up a main share of the barrier lipids in the horny layer?
116502.e: The lipids between the horny cells consist mainly of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids. They arrange themselves in dense layers.
116502.m: Ceramides are important building blocks of the skin barrier.

116503.q: Roughly what pH does the acid mantle of healthy skin surface have?
116503.e: The skin surface is slightly acidic, roughly in the range pH 4.5 to 5.5. This inhibits many pathogens and supports enzymes that build the barrier.
116503.m: Healthy skin is slightly acidic on the surface.

116504.q: Which skin disease is closely linked to a disturbed skin barrier?
116504.e: In atopic eczema the skin barrier is weakened. The skin loses a lot of water, becomes dry and reacts sensitively to irritants and allergens.
116504.m: Atopic eczema goes together with a disturbed skin barrier.

116505.q: Which measurement is often used to test the function of the skin barrier?
116505.e: Transepidermal water loss measures how much water evaporates outwards through the skin. If the barrier is damaged, this value rises.
116505.m: A lot of water loss through the skin shows a disturbed barrier.

116506.q: Roughly how long does it take for the epidermis to renew itself from the basal layer to flaking off?
116506.e: New cells form in the basal layer, move upwards and become keratinised. After about four weeks they flake off at the surface.
116506.m: The epidermis renews itself about once a month.

116507.q: Why can washing very often with soap weaken the skin barrier?
a: It dissolves lipids and shifts the pH
116507.e: Surfactants dissolve skin fats out of the horny layer, and alkaline soaps raise the pH. The skin becomes dry and more prone to irritation.
116507.m: Too much soap removes the skin's fats and weakens its barrier.

116805.q: Which process does the P wave on the ECG show?
116805.e: The P wave arises when excitation spreads from the sinus node across both atria (depolarisation of the atria).
116805.m: The P wave stands for excitation of the atria.

116806.q: What does the T wave on the ECG represent?
116806.e: The T wave shows the recovery of the ventricular muscle from excitation. The spread of excitation in the ventricles, by contrast, is shown by the QRS complex.
116806.m: With the T wave the excitation of the ventricles recovers.

116807.q: What does the PQ interval on the ECG show?
a: How long the excitation takes from the atria to the ventricles
How long a whole heartbeat lasts
How much blood the heart pumps out per beat
116807.e: The PQ interval runs from the start of atrial excitation to the start of ventricular excitation. It shows how fast the excitation is passed on through the AV node.
116807.m: The PQ interval measures conduction from the atria to the ventricles.

116808.q: An ECG runs at 25 mm/s. The distance between two R waves is 20 mm. What is the heart rate?
116808.e: 20 mm divided by 25 mm/s gives 0.8 s per beat. 60 s divided by 0.8 s gives 75 beats per minute.
116808.m: You get the heart rate by dividing 60 seconds by the RR interval in seconds.

116809.q: Who received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1924 for developing the electrocardiogram?
116809.e: The Dutch physiologist Willem Einthoven developed the string galvanometer and with it the modern ECG. He received the Nobel Prize for this in 1924.
116809.m: Willem Einthoven is considered the father of the modern ECG.

116810.q: How many leads does a standard resting ECG include?
116810.e: The standard ECG consists of 6 limb leads (Einthoven and Goldberger) and 6 chest leads according to Wilson (V1 to V6).
116810.m: A standard resting ECG has twelve leads.

116811.q: Why is an ECG recorded immediately when a heart attack is suspected?
a: A heart attack changes the heart's electrical signals in a typical way
The ECG shows blocked arteries as a picture
The ECG measures the blood pressure in the coronary arteries
116811.e: When heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen, it conducts the excitation differently. This can often be seen at once on the ECG, for example as ST elevation.
116811.m: An ECG can quickly reveal a heart attack.

116812.q: Which part of the ECG curve shows the excitation of the ventricles?
116812.e: The QRS complex is the large, sharp spike on the ECG. It arises when excitation spreads through the powerful ventricular muscle.
116812.m: The large QRS spike stands for excitation of the ventricles.

116813.q: What does an ECG basically measure?
a: The blood pressure in the aorta
The blood flow in the veins
The heart sounds over the chest
116813.e: The excitation of heart muscle cells creates electric fields. Electrodes on the skin measure the resulting potential differences in the millivolt range.
116813.m: The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.

116814.q: How fast does the AV node conduct excitation compared with the Purkinje fibres?
a: Not at all, it only conducts backwards
116814.e: In the AV node excitation is conducted at only a few centimetres per second, in the Purkinje fibres at a few metres per second.
116814.m: Conduction is slowest in the AV node and fastest in the Purkinje fibres.

116815.q: What happens to the heartbeat if the sinus node fails and the AV node takes over the rhythm?
116815.e: The AV node can step in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower than that of the sinus node.
116815.m: The AV node is a slower backup pacemaker of the heart.

116816.q: Between which parts of the heart does the AV node pass on the excitation?
a: From the atria to the ventricles
From the ventricles to the aorta
From the lungs to the atria
From the brain to the heart
116816.e: AV stands for atrioventricular, meaning atrium and ventricle. The AV node is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles.
116816.m: The AV node links the atria and ventricles electrically.

116817.q: Why is the excitation briefly delayed in the AV node?
a: So that the ventricles fill before they contract
So that the heart saves energy
So that the blood pressure falls
So that the lungs get more air
116817.e: First the atria contract and pump blood into the ventricles. Only then should the ventricles contract.
116817.m: The delay in the AV node gives the ventricles time to fill.

116818.q: Which examination measures the electrical excitation of the heart?
116818.e: The ECG records the excitation of the heart using electrodes on the skin. Problems with conduction in the AV node show up as longer intervals.
116818.m: The ECG shows the electrical activity of the heart.

116819.q: How does the vagus nerve (parasympathetic system) affect the AV node?
a: It has no effect at all
It makes the AV node the pacemaker
116819.e: The parasympathetic system has a negative dromotropic effect, meaning it delays conduction in the AV node. The sympathetic system, by contrast, speeds it up.
116819.m: The vagus nerve slows conduction in the AV node.

116820.q: Why does the AV node protect the ventricles during atrial fibrillation?
a: It lets only some of the impulses through
116820.e: In atrial fibrillation very many disordered impulses arrive at the AV node. Because of its slow conduction and refractory period, only some of them reach the ventricles.
116820.m: The AV node acts like a filter for atrial impulses that are too fast.

116821.q: Where is the AV node located?
a: At the floor of the right atrium near the septum
In the tip of the left ventricle
In the wall of the aorta
At the opening of the pulmonary veins
116821.e: The AV node lies in the right atrium near the atrial septum, above the transition to the ventricles (in the so-called triangle of Koch).
116821.m: The AV node sits in the right atrium at the border between the atria and ventricles.

116822.q: In which order does normal excitation pass through the heart?
a: Sinus node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres
AV node, sinus node, bundle branches, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
Sinus node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle branches
Purkinje fibres, bundle branches, bundle of His, AV node, sinus node
116822.e: Excitation starts in the sinus node, travels across the atria to the AV node and then via the bundle of His and the bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular muscle.
116822.m: Excitation runs from the sinus node via the AV node to the Purkinje fibres.

116823.q: Which structure is the primary pacemaker of the healthy heart?
116823.e: The sinus node has the highest intrinsic rate of about 60 to 80 per minute and therefore sets the rhythm.
116823.m: In the healthy heart the sinus node sets the rhythm.

116824.q: What is the role of the bundle of His in the heart?
a: It carries the excitation from the AV node to the ventricles
It creates the heart's basic rhythm
It supplies the heart muscle with blood
116824.e: The bundle of His is part of the conduction system. It carries the excitation from the AV node through the septum to the bundle branches. It is named after the Basel doctor Wilhelm His Jr.
116824.m: The bundle of His carries the excitation to the ventricles.

116825.q: What does the heart's conduction system consist of?
a: Smooth muscle cells of the blood vessels
116825.e: The conduction system consists of special heart muscle cells that can excite themselves and pass on excitation quickly. That is why the heart keeps beating even without nerves.
116825.m: The heart produces its excitation with its own specialised muscle cells.

116826.q: What takes over the rhythm if the sinus node fails?
a: The AV node, with a slower rhythm
The lungs, with their breathing rhythm
116826.e: If the sinus node fails, the AV node steps in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower.
116826.m: If the sinus node fails, the slower AV node takes over.

116827.q: Why does the AV node briefly delay passing on the excitation?
a: So that the atria can fill the ventricles first
So that the sinus node can recover
So that the heart valves can open
So that the blood in the lungs can take up oxygen
116827.e: The short delay in the AV node makes sure the atria contract first and press blood into the ventricles. Only after that do the ventricles contract.
116827.m: The AV node briefly holds back so that the ventricles fill first.

116828.q: What is the heart's ability to produce excitation itself without an outside stimulus called?
116828.e: Pacemaker cells slowly depolarise by themselves until a threshold is reached. This property is called automaticity, or the autonomy of the heart.
116828.m: Thanks to automaticity, the heart beats under its own power.

a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
Blood volume divided by stroke volume
116829.e: Cardiac output is the amount of blood that one ventricle pumps out per minute. It is the amount per beat times the number of beats per minute.
116829.m: Cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate.

116830.q: A heart has a stroke volume of 80 ml and beats 60 times a minute. What is the cardiac output?
116830.e: 80 ml times 60 per minute makes 4,800 ml per minute, that is 4.8 litres per minute.
116830.m: For cardiac output, multiply the stroke volume by the heart rate.

116831.q: How much blood does a heart pump per day with a cardiac output of 5 l/min?
116831.e: A day has 24 times 60, that is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 times 5 litres makes 7,200 litres.
116831.m: The heart pumps several thousand litres of blood every day.

116832.q: During exercise an athlete has a stroke volume of 150 ml and a heart rate of 180 per minute. What is his cardiac output?
116832.e: 150 ml times 180 per minute makes 27,000 ml per minute, that is 27 litres per minute.
116832.m: During exercise, cardiac output can rise to several times the resting value.

116833.q: Roughly how large is the cardiac output of a healthy adult at rest?
116833.e: At rest, a healthy adult's heart pumps out about 5 litres of blood per minute. That is roughly the body's entire amount of blood.
116833.m: At rest the heart pumps about five litres of blood per minute.

116834.q: How does the heart increase its cardiac output during physical exercise?
a: Through higher stroke volume and higher heart rate
Only through a lower heart rate
116834.e: During exercise the heart beats faster and pumps out more blood per beat. Together these greatly increase the amount of blood per minute.
116834.m: More beats and more blood per beat increase cardiac output.

116835.q: Cardiac output can be calculated as oxygen uptake divided by the difference in oxygen between arterial and venous blood. What is it at 250 ml/min and 50 ml per litre of blood?
116835.e: 250 ml/min divided by 50 ml/l gives 5 l/min. This method is called the Fick principle.
116835.m: According to Fick, you divide the oxygen uptake by the arteriovenous difference.

116836.q: What does the cardiac index show?
a: Cardiac output per square metre of body surface
Heart rate per kilogram of body weight
Stroke volume per litre of blood
116836.e: The cardiac index relates cardiac output to body surface area. This makes it easier to compare large and small people.
116836.m: The cardiac index makes cardiac output comparable between people of different sizes.

116837.q: The end-diastolic volume is 130 ml and the end-systolic volume is 60 ml. What is the stroke volume?
116837.e: The stroke volume is the difference between the filling at the end of diastole and the remaining volume at the end of systole: 130 ml minus 60 ml makes 70 ml.
116837.m: Stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume.

116838.q: The stroke volume is 60 ml and the end-diastolic volume is 120 ml. What is the ejection fraction?
116838.e: The ejection fraction is the stroke volume divided by the end-diastolic volume: 60 divided by 120 gives 0.5, that is 50 %.
116838.m: The ejection fraction shows what share of the filling is pumped out.

116839.q: What does the Frank-Starling mechanism state?
a: Greater filling leads to a larger stroke volume
A higher heart rate always lowers stroke volume
The heart always pumps the same amount of blood
The sinus node adapts to blood pressure
116839.e: If the ventricle is filled and stretched more during diastole, it then contracts more strongly. In this way the heart automatically adapts to changing return of blood.
116839.m: According to Frank-Starling, a fuller heart pumps out more blood.

116840.q: What is meant by the afterload of the heart?
a: The resistance to pumping out blood
The filling of the ventricle before contraction
The blood left behind after the beat
116840.e: Afterload is the force the ventricle has to overcome when pumping out blood, mainly the pressure in the aorta. If it rises, stroke volume falls with the same force.
116840.m: Afterload is the resistance the heart pumps against.

116841.q: Roughly how large is the stroke volume of a healthy adult at rest?
116841.e: At rest each ventricle pumps out about 70 ml of blood per beat, and much more in trained people.
116841.m: At rest each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per beat.

116842.q: Why do endurance athletes often have a low resting heart rate?
a: Their cardiac output is much smaller
116842.e: A trained heart is stronger and pumps out more blood per beat. So it needs fewer beats per minute for the same cardiac output.
116842.m: A larger stroke volume allows a lower resting heart rate.

116843.q: How do you calculate cardiac output, the amount of blood the heart pumps per minute?
a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
116843.e: With 70 ml per beat and 70 beats per minute, the heart pumps about 4.9 litres of blood per minute.
116843.m: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.

116844.q: What is called the preload of the heart?
a: The stretch of the ventricle at the end of filling
The number of heartbeats per minute
The resistance in the lung vessels
116844.e: Preload corresponds to the filling and stretching of the ventricle at the end of diastole. It depends mainly on the return of blood through the veins.
116844.m: Preload is the stretching of the ventricle by the incoming blood.

116845.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
a: From the root of the aorta
116845.e: The two coronary arteries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve. In this way they are the first to receive oxygen-rich blood.
116845.m: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta just above the aortic valve.

116846.q: How many coronary arteries branch off directly from the aorta?
116846.e: A left and a right coronary artery arise just above the aortic valve. The left one soon divides into two large branches.
116846.m: Two coronary arteries arise from the aorta.

116847.q: In which phase of the heartbeat is the wall of the left ventricle mainly supplied with blood?
116847.e: In systole the tensed heart muscle squeezes the vessels in the wall. That is why most blood flows in the relaxation phase.
116847.m: The left heart muscle is mainly supplied with blood in diastole.

116848.q: Which disease is caused by the narrowing of the coronary arteries as a result of arteriosclerosis?
116848.e: Deposits in the vessel wall narrow the coronary arteries. The heart muscle then gets too little oxygen during exertion.
116848.m: Coronary heart disease is caused by narrowed coronary arteries.

116849.q: What is the typical feeling of tightness in the chest called when the heart muscle lacks oxygen?
116849.e: Angina pectoris literally means tightness of the chest. It typically occurs during exertion, when narrowed coronary arteries cannot deliver enough blood.
116849.m: Angina pectoris is a warning sign of poor blood supply to the heart.

116850.q: Which examination uses contrast medium to make the coronary arteries visible on an X-ray?
116850.e: Contrast medium is injected directly into the coronary arteries through a cardiac catheter. Narrowings can then be seen on the X-ray.
116850.m: Coronary angiography shows narrowed coronary arteries on an X-ray.

116851.q: Why does heart muscle usually die when a coronary artery is suddenly blocked?
a: There are hardly any adequate bypass routes
The blood flows backwards into the lungs
The heart muscle stores too much oxygen
116851.e: The connections between the coronary branches are usually not enough to replace a blocked vessel quickly. They are called functional end arteries; the area supplied dies, causing a heart attack.
116851.m: Coronary arteries have hardly any adequate bypass routes.

116852.q: Why can a heart attack trigger heart rhythm disorders?
a: The conduction system can also be left without blood
The lungs press on the heart
116852.e: The coronary arteries also supply the sinus node and the AV node. If they lack blood, conduction can be disturbed; the AV node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery.
116852.m: A heart attack can also affect the heart's conduction system.

116853.q: What is special about a bioresorbable stent?
a: It is pulled out again after a week
116853.e: Bioresorbable vessel supports are made of degradable materials such as lactic acid polymers or magnesium. After the healing phase the body breaks them down.
116853.m: A bioresorbable stent is broken down by the body.

116854.q: Who carried out the first balloon dilation of a coronary artery in a human in Zurich in 1977?
116854.e: In 1977, at University Hospital Zurich, Andreas Grüntzig widened a narrowed coronary artery with a balloon catheter for the first time. This marked the start of interventional cardiology.
116854.m: The first coronary balloon dilation was achieved in Zurich in 1977.

116855.q: What is the coating of a drug-eluting stent for?
a: It stops the vessel from growing closed again
It dissolves calcium from the aorta
It colours the stent on the X-ray
116855.e: The stent slowly releases active substances that slow cell division in the vessel wall. This lowers the risk of renewed narrowing (restenosis).
116855.m: Drug-eluting stents reduce the risk of restenosis.

116856.q: Why do patients usually receive two platelet inhibitors after a stent is implanted?
116856.e: Platelets can stick to the foreign material and form a clot. Dual antiplatelet therapy, for example with acetylsalicylic acid and clopidogrel, prevents this.
116856.m: After a stent, platelet inhibitors protect against clots.

116857.q: Through which access point is a coronary stent often inserted today?
a: Through the artery at the wrist
Through a vein in the neck
116857.e: Today the radial artery at the wrist is often punctured, or alternatively the groin artery. The stent travels to the heart through a catheter.
116857.m: A coronary stent is brought to the heart through the arteries with a catheter.

116858.q: How is a balloon-expandable stent opened up at the narrowing?
116858.e: The stent sits folded up on a balloon catheter. When the balloon is filled under pressure, the stent expands and presses against the vessel wall.
116858.m: A balloon presses the stent against the vessel wall.

116859.q: Who is the term “stent” named after?
116859.e: The name goes back to the English dentist Charles Stent, who developed an impression material in the 19th century. His name was later used for support materials.
116859.m: The stent owes its name to an English dentist.

116860.q: What is done in a heart bypass operation?
a: A narrowing is bypassed with a replacement vessel
116860.e: A vessel is connected so that the blood flows around the narrowed part of the coronary artery. Bypass means a way around.
116860.m: A bypass leads the blood past a narrowing.

116861.q: Which disease most often makes a heart bypass operation necessary?
a: Coronary arteries narrowed by hardening of the arteries
A heartbeat that is too slow
A hole in the septum of the heart
116861.e: In coronary heart disease, deposits build up in the coronary arteries. The heart muscle gets too little blood, and a bypass leads the blood past the narrowing.
116861.m: A bypass helps with narrowed coronary arteries.

116862.q: From which part of the body is a piece of vein often taken for a vein bypass on the heart?
116862.e: The superficial great saphenous vein in the leg is long, easy to reach and can be spared. A piece of it is inserted between the aorta and the coronary artery.
116862.m: Vein bypasses often use a vein from the leg.

116863.q: Which machine temporarily takes over the work of the heart and lungs in many bypass operations?
116863.e: The heart-lung machine pumps the blood and enriches it with oxygen. This allows surgeons to operate on the stopped heart.
116863.m: The heart-lung machine replaces the heart and lungs during the operation.

116864.q: How is the chest usually opened for a classic bypass operation?
116864.e: In a median sternotomy, the breastbone is cut through lengthwise. Afterwards it is closed again with wire loops.
116864.m: For a classic bypass operation, the breastbone is opened lengthwise.

a: An operation on the beating heart
An operation without a replacement vessel
116865.e: In the off-pump method no heart-lung machine is used. A stabiliser keeps the stitching site still on the beating heart.
116865.m: In an off-pump bypass the heart keeps beating during the operation.

116866.q: Which gentler treatment is often chosen instead of a bypass operation for narrowed coronary arteries?
a: A stent is inserted through a catheter
116866.e: Through a catheter in the groin or at the wrist, the narrowing is widened with a balloon and kept open with a stent. The chest does not have to be opened for this.
116866.m: A stent keeps a narrowed coronary artery open without major surgery.

116867.q: What does the German abbreviation ACVB stand for in heart surgery?
116867.e: ACVB refers to a bypass in which a vein leads from the aorta to the coronary artery beyond the narrowing. In English the operation is called CABG.
116867.m: An ACVB connects the aorta to a coronary artery via a vein.

116868.q: What is meant by heart failure?
a: The heart does not pump enough blood for the body's needs
The heart has a hole in the septum
The heart is wrapped in fat
116868.e: In heart failure the heart can no longer supply the body with enough blood, or only at raised filling pressures.
116868.m: In heart failure the heart's pumping power is not enough.

116869.q: Which symptom is typical of left-sided heart failure?
a: Breathlessness from congestion in the lungs
Strong thirst from high blood sugar
116869.e: If the left ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up into the lung vessels. Fluid leaks into the tissue, causing breathlessness and, in extreme cases, pulmonary oedema.
116869.m: A weak left ventricle leads to blood backing up in the lungs.

116870.q: Which sign points to right-sided heart failure?
a: Coughing up blood in the morning
116870.e: If the right ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up in the body's veins. This causes oedema in the legs, swollen neck veins and a congested liver.
116870.m: In right-sided heart failure, blood backs up in the body's veins.

116871.q: How can you tell severe heart failure from mild heart failure?
a: Breathlessness is present even at rest
Breathlessness only occurs during a marathon
There are no symptoms at all
116871.e: Doctors classify heart failure by its symptoms. In the most severe class, breathlessness and exhaustion are present even at rest.
116871.m: In severe heart failure, symptoms are present even at rest.

116872.q: What does the ejection fraction of the heart show?
a: The share of blood the ventricle pumps out per beat
The number of heartbeats per minute
The blood pressure in the aorta
The size of the heart in centimetres
116872.e: The ejection fraction shows what percentage of its filling the left ventricle pumps out in one beat. In healthy people it is over 50 per cent.
116872.m: The ejection fraction measures the pumping strength of the ventricle.

116873.q: Which examination assesses the heart's pumping power without an invasive procedure?
116873.e: A heart ultrasound shows the ventricles and valves moving. This makes it possible to estimate how strongly the heart pumps.
116873.m: A heart ultrasound shows how well the heart pumps.

116874.q: Why should people with heart failure weigh themselves every day?
a: A rapid gain shows fluid retention
They have to lose weight every day
116874.e: A gain of more than about 1 kg per day or 2 kg in a few days usually points to fluid in the body. The treatment must then be adjusted.
116874.m: Sudden weight gain can show that heart failure is getting worse.

116875.q: Which group of medicines flushes out water in heart failure?
116875.e: Diuretics increase the excretion of salt and water through the kidneys. This reduces oedema and breathlessness.
116875.m: Diuretics help get rid of excess water.

116876.q: From which plant does the historical heart medicine digitalis come?
116876.e: In 1785 the English doctor William Withering described the effect of foxglove leaves on dropsy. The active substances increase the strength of the heart.

a: The electrical activity of the heart
The blood pressure in the arteries
The size of the heart's ventricles
116877.e: The electrocardiogram uses electrodes on the skin to measure the electrical signals that trigger each heartbeat. This makes rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation visible.
116877.m: An ECG records the heart's electrical signals.

116878.q: Which serious complication is a particular risk with atrial fibrillation?
a: A stroke caused by a clot
116878.e: In the fibrillating atria, especially the left atrial appendage, blood flows slowly and can clot. A clot that breaks free can block an artery in the brain.
116878.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

116879.q: What is typically noticeable when feeling the pulse of someone with atrial fibrillation?
a: The pulse is very slow and completely regular
No pulse can be felt at all
The pulse always beats exactly 60 times a minute
116879.e: The atria twitch chaotically and the ventricles receive the signals at irregular intervals. That is why the pulse is completely irregular.
116879.m: Atrial fibrillation makes the pulse irregular.

116880.q: Which medicines do many people with atrial fibrillation take to prevent a stroke?
116880.e: Blood clots can form in the fibrillating atria. Anticoagulants make this less likely and so lower the risk of stroke.
116880.m: Blood thinners protect against stroke in atrial fibrillation.

a: A targeted electric shock that normalises the rhythm
An operation on the heart valves
116881.e: Under a short anaesthetic, an electric shock synchronised with the ECG is given. All cells are excited at the same time, and afterwards the sinus node often takes over again.
116881.m: Cardioversion uses an electric shock to put the heart back into sinus rhythm.

116882.q: Which structure sets the rhythm in the healthy heart, which is disturbed in atrial fibrillation?
116882.e: The sinus node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker. In atrial fibrillation, chaotic excitation in the atria drowns out its rhythm.
116882.m: Normally the sinus node sets the heart's rhythm.

116883.q: Which factors particularly increase the risk of atrial fibrillation?
a: Older age and high blood pressure
Young age and a low pulse
116883.e: Atrial fibrillation becomes much more common with age. High blood pressure, being overweight, diabetes and a lot of alcohol also raise the risk.
116883.m: Age and high blood pressure are important risk factors for atrial fibrillation.

116884.q: How common is atrial fibrillation compared with other persistent heart rhythm disorders?
a: It is one of the rarest
116884.e: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder. The risk rises clearly with age.
116884.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder.

116885.q: Roughly how long does the battery of a modern pacemaker last?
116885.e: Modern pacemakers use very little power. When the battery runs out, the whole device is replaced in a small procedure.
116885.m: A pacemaker usually lasts about a decade.

116886.q: For which disorder is a pacemaker typically fitted?
a: A heartbeat that is too slow
116886.e: A pacemaker gives off electrical impulses when the heart beats too slowly, for example with AV block or sinus node disease.
116886.m: A pacemaker mainly helps when the heartbeat is too slow.

116887.q: What should people with a pacemaker watch out for in everyday life?
a: Not holding strong magnets or mobile phones directly over the device
116887.e: Strong magnetic fields can disturb how the pacemaker works. That is why mobile phones or headphones with magnets are kept a little way from the device.
116887.m: A pacemaker needs to be kept away from strong magnets.

116888.q: Which type of battery is usually used in modern pacemakers?
116888.e: Lithium batteries are small, very long-lasting and hardly discharge by themselves. With them, a pacemaker usually lasts many years.
116888.m: Pacemakers are usually powered by lithium batteries.

116889.q: By which route do the leads of a classic pacemaker reach the heart?
a: Through a vein below the collarbone
Through the aorta from the groin
Through the skin directly into the heart
116889.e: The leads are pushed through a vein below the collarbone into the right atrium or right ventricle. The device lies under the skin.
116889.m: Pacemaker leads are guided through a vein into the right side of the heart.

116890.q: What is special about a capsule pacemaker?
a: It sits directly in the right ventricle without wires
It is worn on the wrist
It is swallowed and passed out again
116890.e: The wireless capsule pacemaker is about the size of a large vitamin capsule and is placed in the right ventricle by catheter. No lead wires are then needed.
116890.m: A capsule pacemaker needs no wires.

116891.q: What is a biventricular pacemaker (CRT) for?
a: It synchronises both ventricles in heart failure
It dissolves blood clots in the atrium
It replaces a faulty heart valve
116891.e: In some forms of heart failure the ventricles contract out of step. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy stimulates both ventricles at the same time and so improves pumping.
116891.m: CRT brings both ventricles back into step.

116892.q: What can an implantable defibrillator (ICD) do in addition to a pacemaker?
a: End ventricular fibrillation with a shock
116892.e: An ICD recognises life-threatening fast rhythm disorders such as ventricular fibrillation and then gives an electric shock.
116892.m: An ICD can end ventricular fibrillation with an electric shock.

116893.q: With classic cold storage, roughly how long may a donor heart be outside the body?
116893.e: When cooled on ice, the heart should usually be supplied with blood again within about four hours. That is why removal, transport and implantation must happen very quickly.
116893.m: A donor heart must be implanted within a few hours.

116894.q: In which city did the world's first heart transplant take place in 1967?
116894.e: In December 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard transplanted a human heart for the first time in Cape Town. Switzerland followed in 1969 in Zurich.
116894.m: The first heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town in 1967.

116895.q: Why do people have to take medicines for life after a heart transplant?
a: So that the immune system does not reject the donor heart
So that the heart grows faster
So that the blood becomes thicker
So that the scar heals more neatly
116895.e: The immune system recognises the donor heart as foreign. Medicines damp down the defence so that it does not attack the heart.
116895.m: After a transplant, medicines prevent rejection.

116896.q: Why does a transplanted heart react to exertion with a faster pulse only after a delay?
a: It is not connected to nerves
It is smaller than the old heart
116896.e: The nerves are cut during the transplant. So the heart only speeds up once hormones such as adrenaline rise in the blood.
116896.m: A transplanted heart is controlled mainly by hormones.

116897.q: How is rejection of a donor heart often monitored?
a: With small tissue samples from the heart muscle
116897.e: In an endomyocardial biopsy, tiny samples are taken from the inner wall of the heart through a catheter. Signs of rejection can be seen under the microscope.
116897.m: Heart muscle biopsies show the start of rejection.

116898.q: From which animal did the heart come that was transplanted into a living human for the first time in the USA in 2022?
116898.e: In January 2022, a man with severe heart disease in Maryland received a genetically modified pig heart. He lived for about two more months.
116898.m: Transplanting animal organs into humans is called xenotransplantation.

116899.q: What is a ventricular assist device (VAD) often used for before a transplant?
a: To bridge the time until a donor heart is available
116899.e: An implanted pump supports the weakened ventricle. This lets people with severe heart disease bridge the often long wait for a donor heart.
116899.m: A VAD can bridge the wait for a donor heart.

116900.q: In a usual heart transplant, what happens to the diseased heart?
a: It is removed and replaced by the donor heart
It is repaired and put back
It is moved into the abdomen
It is frozen and returned later
116900.e: The diseased heart is taken out and the donor heart is sewn in its place. Specialists call this orthotopic transplantation.
116900.m: In a usual heart transplant, the donor heart replaces the old heart.

116901.q: Apart from the coronary arteries, in which vessel are stents also often used?
a: In the portal vein of the liver
In the skin veins of the hand
116901.e: Stents are also used for narrowings of the carotid artery and the leg and kidney arteries. Everywhere the aim is to restore blood flow.
116901.m: Stents keep open not only coronary arteries but other arteries too.

116902.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the sinus node?
116902.e: Through noradrenaline the sympathetic system has a positive chronotropic effect. The pacemaker cells depolarise faster and the heart beats more quickly.
116902.m: The sympathetic nervous system speeds up the heartbeat.

116903.q: Roughly what share of cardiac output flows through the coronary arteries at rest?
116903.e: The heart makes up only about half a per cent of body weight but receives about 5 % of cardiac output. Even at rest it extracts a lot of the oxygen from the blood.
116903.m: The heart receives about five per cent of cardiac output for itself.

117200.q: In which blood vessels is blood pressure highest?
a: In the large arteries close to the heart
In the veins of the feet
117200.e: The left ventricle pumps blood at high pressure into the aorta and the large arteries. On its way through the vessels the pressure keeps falling.
117200.m: Blood pressure is highest in the arteries close to the heart.

117201.q: What does the systolic blood pressure value refer to?
a: The highest pressure while the heart is pumping out blood
The lowest pressure in the filling phase
The pressure in the pulmonary veins
The pressure in the right atrium
117201.e: The systolic value is the peak pressure in the arteries when the left ventricle pumps out blood. The diastolic value is the lowest pressure in the relaxation phase.
117201.m: The systolic value is the upper blood pressure value.

117203.q: When measuring blood pressure by hand, what do you hear with the stethoscope in the crook of the elbow?
a: Sounds of blood flowing in the artery
117203.e: When the cuff pressure is slowly released, blood spurts through the squeezed artery. These sounds show the upper and lower blood pressure values.
117203.m: When measuring blood pressure, you hear blood flowing through the artery.

117204.q: According to the “Ohm's law” of the circulation, which two quantities determine mean blood pressure?
117204.e: Blood pressure roughly equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. If one of them rises, the pressure rises too.
117204.m: Blood pressure comes from cardiac output times vessel resistance.

117205.q: Mean arterial pressure is roughly the diastolic value plus one third of the difference to the systolic value. What is it at 120/80 mmHg?
117205.e: 80 + (120 minus 80) / 3 gives about 93 mmHg. The mean pressure is closer to the lower value because the heart spends longer relaxing than contracting.
117205.m: Mean pressure is closer to the diastolic than to the systolic value.

117206.q: The flow resistance of a vessel depends on the fourth power of the radius. By what factor does it rise if the radius is halved?
117206.e: Resistance is inversely proportional to r to the power of 4. If the radius is halved, resistance rises by 2 to the power of 4, that is 16 times.
117206.m: Even small narrowings of a vessel raise resistance a lot.

117207.q: Which hormone from the adrenal medulla makes blood pressure and pulse rise quickly under stress?
117207.e: Under stress the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. It speeds up the heartbeat and narrows many blood vessels, so blood pressure rises.
117207.m: Adrenaline drives up blood pressure and pulse.

117208.q: Which organ is most important for regulating blood pressure in the long term?
117208.e: The kidney controls blood volume through the excretion of salt and water. In this way it determines blood pressure over days and weeks.
117208.m: The kidney regulates blood pressure in the long run.

117209.q: Which stimulus do baroreceptors in the vessel wall react to?
117209.e: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors. If blood pressure rises, the vessel wall is stretched more and they fire more often.
117209.m: Baroreceptors measure blood pressure through the stretching of the wall.

117210.q: Where are the most important pressure sensors (baroreceptors) for arterial blood pressure?
a: In the carotid artery and the aortic arch
In the veins of the legs
In the alveoli of the lungs
117210.e: The most important arterial baroreceptors sit at the fork of the carotid artery and in the aortic arch, so close to the heart and on the way to the brain.
117210.m: The carotid artery and aortic arch contain the most important pressure sensors.

117211.q: In which part of the brain is the cardiovascular centre that processes the signals from the baroreceptors?
117211.e: The cardiovascular centre lies in the medulla oblongata. There the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are adjusted.
117211.m: The cardiovascular centre sits in the medulla oblongata.

117212.q: What does the baroreceptor reflex do when blood pressure suddenly rises?
117212.e: More stretch leads to more signals to the cardiovascular centre. It damps down the sympathetic system and activates the vagus, so heart rate and pressure fall.
117212.m: When pressure is high, the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart.

117213.q: By which route do the baroreceptors' signals reach the cardiovascular centre?
a: Through hormones in the blood to the kidney
Through the spinal cord to the cerebellum
Through the lymph to the spleen
117213.e: The baroreceptors send their signals through cranial nerves such as the vagus to the cardiovascular centre in the brainstem. This lets the body react within seconds.
117213.m: Baroreceptors report the pressure to the brainstem through nerves.

117214.q: Why can strong pressure on the side of the carotid artery slow the heart?
a: The pressure sensors wrongly report high blood pressure
The carotid artery is completely blocked
The heart gets too little oxygen
The larynx presses on the heart
117214.e: Pressure from outside stretches the wall of the carotid artery. The brain interprets this as a rise in blood pressure and slows the heart by reflex.
117214.m: Pressure on the carotid artery can slow the heart.

117215.q: Which kind of blood pressure regulation is the baroreceptor reflex mainly responsible for?
117215.e: The reflex evens out short-term fluctuations, for example when standing up. With permanently high pressure the receptors adjust to a higher level.
117215.m: The baroreceptor reflex acts quickly, but only in the short term.

117216.q: What happens to the baroreceptors when blood pressure is permanently raised?
117216.e: In chronic hypertension the set point of the baroreceptors shifts upwards. The high pressure is then no longer reported as a deviation.
117216.m: Baroreceptors get used to permanently high pressure.

117217.q: In which organ is the enzyme renin made?
117217.e: Renin is made by specialised cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the kidney. They sit on the arterioles leading into the glomeruli.

117218.q: Which stimulus mainly leads to the release of renin?
a: Falling blood pressure in the kidney
117218.e: If the pressure in the kidney vessels or the amount of salt at the macula densa falls, more renin is released. The sympathetic system also stimulates the release.
117218.m: Low pressure in the kidney triggers renin release.

117219.q: Which protein does renin split into angiotensin I?
117219.e: Renin splits angiotensinogen, which is made in the liver. This produces angiotensin I, which has hardly any effect yet.
117219.m: Renin cuts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

117220.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II?
117220.e: ACE, mainly on the lining of the lung vessels, turns angiotensin I into the highly effective angiotensin II.
117220.m: ACE produces the active angiotensin II.

117221.e: Aldosterone is made in the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa. Angiotensin II stimulates its production.
117221.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

117222.q: What does aldosterone do in the kidney tubules?
117222.e: In the collecting duct, aldosterone promotes the reabsorption of sodium and the excretion of potassium. Water follows the sodium, and blood volume rises.
117222.m: Aldosterone keeps sodium, and with it water, in the body.

117223.q: Which side effect is typical of ACE inhibitors?
a: A green discolouration of the skin
Loss of the sense of smell
117223.e: ACE also breaks down bradykinin. If it is inhibited, bradykinin builds up, which often triggers a dry cough.
117223.m: ACE inhibitors often cause an irritating cough.

117224.q: How do blood pressure medicines of the sartan group work?
a: They block the angiotensin II receptor
They inhibit renin production in the liver
117224.e: Sartans such as losartan occupy the AT1 receptor. Angiotensin II can then no longer narrow the vessels.
117224.m: Sartans protect the vessels from angiotensin II.

117225.q: From which natural model was the first ACE inhibitor, captopril, developed?
a: From the venom of a lancehead viper
117225.e: Peptides that inhibit ACE were found in the venom of the Brazilian snake Bothrops jararaca. They served as the model for captopril.
117225.m: A snake venom led to ACE inhibitors.

117226.q: From which values measured at the doctor's surgery does the usual European definition speak of high blood pressure?
117226.e: According to European guidelines, a value of 140/90 mmHg or more measured repeatedly at the surgery counts as hypertension. Values below that can still be raised.
117226.m: From 140/90 mmHg it is called high blood pressure.

117227.q: Why is high blood pressure often called a “silent killer”?
a: It causes no symptoms for a long time
117227.e: Many people affected feel nothing for years while their vessels, heart and kidneys are already being damaged. That is why regular measurements are important.
117227.m: High blood pressure often does harm without causing pain.

117228.q: What is the most common form of high blood pressure without a single identifiable cause called?
117228.e: In about nine out of ten people affected, no single cause is found. This is called primary or essential hypertension.
117228.m: Most high blood pressure has no single cause.

117229.q: Which organ can cause secondary hypertension if it makes too much aldosterone?
117229.e: The adrenal cortex makes the hormone aldosterone. If there is too much of it, the body holds back sodium and water and blood pressure rises.
117229.m: Too much aldosterone from the adrenal gland raises blood pressure.

117230.q: How does the left ventricle react to years of raised blood pressure?
a: It shrinks to the size of an atrium
117230.e: The heart constantly has to pump against higher pressure. The muscle grows as with training, causing left ventricular hypertrophy.
117230.m: High blood pressure thickens the wall of the left ventricle.

117231.q: Which dietary measure has been shown to lower blood pressure in many people?
117231.e: A lot of sodium binds water in the body and so increases blood volume. A diet lower in salt lowers blood pressure in many people affected.
117231.m: Less salt often helps against high blood pressure.

117232.q: What is 24-hour blood pressure monitoring for?
a: It shows the pattern over day and night
It measures the pressure in the lungs
117232.e: A portable device takes measurements at intervals all day and during the night. This reveals, for example, white coat hypertension or a missing fall in pressure at night.
117232.m: Long-term monitoring shows blood pressure in everyday life.

a: Very high blood pressure with acute organ damage
Slightly raised blood pressure without symptoms
A sudden drop in blood pressure
A high pulse with normal blood pressure
117233.e: In a hypertensive emergency, blood pressure is greatly raised and acutely damages organs such as the brain, heart or kidneys. It must be treated in hospital immediately.
117233.m: A hypertensive emergency needs immediate treatment.

117234.q: Which organ can be so damaged by years of high blood pressure that dialysis becomes necessary?
117234.e: High pressure damages the fine vessels of the renal corpuscles. In the long term kidney function can fall so much that blood cleaning by dialysis is needed.
117234.m: High blood pressure can destroy the kidneys.

117235.q: From which values do doctors usually speak of low blood pressure in adults?
117235.e: Values below about 100/60 mmHg usually count as hypotension. However, many people with such values have no symptoms.
117235.m: Low blood pressure is below about 100/60 mmHg.

117236.q: What is a drop in blood pressure that occurs when standing up quickly called?
117236.e: When you stand up, blood sinks into the legs. If the circulation reacts too slowly, the pressure falls and you feel dizzy.
117236.m: Dizziness on standing up comes from a drop in blood pressure.

117237.q: How does a doctor check whether the circulation reacts well when standing up?
a: Blood pressure and pulse are measured lying down and then standing
Temperature is measured before and after eating
The person is made to run for ten minutes
Blood sugar is measured while sitting
117237.e: In the so-called Schellong test, blood pressure and pulse lying down and standing are compared. If blood pressure drops sharply, there is an orthostatic disorder.
117237.m: A lying-standing test checks the circulation's reaction to standing up.

117238.q: What is a brief loss of consciousness due to a temporary lack of blood flow to the brain called?
117238.e: In a syncope, blood pressure briefly falls so much that the brain gets too little blood. Lying down, people usually recover quickly.
117238.m: The medical term for fainting is syncope.

117239.q: What helps many people with low blood pressure in everyday life?
a: Drinking enough and standing up slowly
Taking hot baths for as long as possible
Drinking little and standing up quickly
117239.e: Enough fluid increases blood volume. Standing up slowly gives the circulation time to adjust.
117239.m: Drinking and standing up slowly help with low blood pressure.

117240.q: Why can compression stockings help with low blood pressure?
a: They stop blood from pooling in the leg veins
117240.e: Pressure from outside reduces the diameter of the leg veins. This lets more blood flow back to the heart and keeps the pressure more stable.
117240.m: Compression stockings stop blood from staying in the legs.

117241.q: Which life-threatening condition with a sharp drop in blood pressure can develop after heavy blood loss?
117241.e: If a lot of blood volume is missing, the heart cannot pump out enough. Blood pressure falls and organs are no longer adequately supplied.
117241.m: Heavy blood loss can trigger shock.

117242.q: How does the body normally react to a drop in blood pressure on standing up?
a: The pulse rises and vessels narrow
The pulse falls and vessels widen
117242.e: Less stretching of the baroreceptors activates the sympathetic system. Heart rate and vessel tension increase, and blood pressure is maintained.
117242.m: When you stand up, the body speeds up the heart.

a: A blocked blood vessel in the brain
117244.e: About four out of five strokes are ischaemic. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain, and the tissue beyond it no longer gets oxygen.
117244.m: A clot usually causes the stroke.

117245.q: In the FAST test, what does the letter T stand for?
a: The time until you call the emergency number
117245.e: FAST stands for Face, Arms, Speech and Time. The T reminds you to call the emergency number immediately, because every minute counts.
117245.m: With a stroke, every minute counts.

117246.q: What is a stroke called that is caused by a blood vessel in the brain bursting?
117246.e: In a haemorrhagic stroke, blood leaks into the brain tissue. The most common cause is blood pressure that has been too high for a long time.
117246.m: A brain haemorrhage is a haemorrhagic stroke.

117247.q: Which treatment dissolves the blood clot with medicines in an ischaemic stroke?
117247.e: In thrombolysis a substance that dissolves the clot is injected. It is only possible within a narrow time window after the symptoms begin.
117247.m: Thrombolysis dissolves clots in the brain.

117248.q: Up to how many hours after symptoms begin is thrombolysis usually possible for a stroke?
117248.e: Thrombolysis is usually used up to about 4.5 hours after symptoms begin. After that the risks of bleeding outweigh the benefits.
117248.m: There is only a little time for thrombolysis in a stroke.

117249.q: What is done in a mechanical thrombectomy?
a: The clot is pulled out with a catheter
Part of the skull is replaced
117249.e: Through a catheter from the groin, the clot is removed from the artery in the brain. The method is suitable for blockages of large vessels.
117249.m: In a thrombectomy the clot is taken out.

117250.q: Which heart rhythm disorder is a common cause of blood clots that trigger a stroke?
117250.e: In atrial fibrillation the atrium no longer contracts properly. Clots form in the still blood and can be washed into the brain.
117250.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

117251.q: What is a transient ischaemic attack?
a: Brief stroke symptoms that disappear quickly
117251.e: In a TIA, signs of a stroke appear that usually go away within minutes. It is considered an urgent warning sign of a coming stroke.
117251.m: A TIA is a serious warning signal.

117252.q: Where does the blood clot in a pulmonary embolism usually come from?
a: From a deep vein in the leg
117252.e: Usually a clot breaks free from a deep vein thrombosis in the leg or pelvis. It reaches the pulmonary arteries through the right side of the heart.
117252.m: Pulmonary embolisms usually begin in the leg veins.

117253.q: Through which ventricle of the heart does a clot from the leg veins reach the lungs?
117253.e: Venous blood flows through the vena cava into the right atrium and right ventricle. From there it is pumped into the pulmonary artery.
117253.m: A venous clot passes through the right side of the heart.

117254.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of a pulmonary embolism?
117254.e: Typical signs are sudden breathlessness, pain when breathing and a fast pulse. Large embolisms can lead to circulatory failure.
117254.m: Sudden breathlessness can point to a pulmonary embolism.

117255.q: Which factor encourages a thrombosis to form?
a: Good blood flow to the skin
117255.e: Rudolf Virchow named three causes: damage to the vessel wall, slowed blood flow and increased clotting of the blood. This is called Virchow's triad.

117256.q: Which blood test helps rule out a pulmonary embolism when suspicion is low?
117256.e: D-dimers are breakdown products of fibrin. If the value is normal and the probability is low, a pulmonary embolism is very unlikely.
117256.m: Normal D-dimers speak against a fresh thrombosis.

117257.q: Which imaging method is usually used today to detect a pulmonary embolism?
117257.e: In CT angiography contrast medium is injected. Clots in the pulmonary arteries then show up as gaps.
117257.m: CT angiography shows clots in the pulmonary arteries.

117258.q: Which group of medicines is the basis of treatment for a pulmonary embolism?
117258.e: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop the clot from growing and new ones from forming. The body can then break down the plug itself.
117258.m: Anticoagulants are the basis of embolism treatment.
